articles.headline: GTA 6 features the series' first non-binary character, says actor Jesse James Rose, and players can't hurt them
keyFacts: Actor Jesse James Rose announced on Instagram that they play Grand Theft Auto 6's first non-binary character, a museum curator role.
Rose stated that developers implemented protections to ensure players cannot inflict in-game violence against the museum curator character.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is available now on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S after launching on Thursday.
body: Grand Theft Auto 6 features the first non-binary character in the series' history, according to actor Jesse James Rose, who plays the role of a museum curator in the game.
"I can FINALLY share that I play the first-ever nonbinary character in the Grand Theft Auto franchise!" Rose wrote on Instagram.
"Absolutely wild to find out THIS was the super-secret game I spent weeks and 17 NDAs filming 3 years ago."

"I shot this back in my they/them days, and everyone on production ensured I was comfortable and gendered correctly," Rose wrote. The project was kept so secret that Rose wasn't told what it was during filming and only recently learned it was GTA 6.
"GTA was one of the most inclusive & caring sets I've ever been on," they added.

The role was shot entirely through motion capture, which meant wearing "a unitard made of dots every day". Rose also says steps were taken to protect the character in-game: "To mitigate anti-trans violence, I was assured that players would not be able to inflict violence against my character."

A whole day of the shoot was spent scanning Rose's face, including hours of pulling different expressions. At one point Rose couldn't move a particular muscle, and worried the scan had been ruined, but the director was thrilled.
"That right there is exactly why we'll never use AI," he said, according to Rose. "A computer could never come up with the face you just made."
"Remember, in a world consumed with Generative AI, the largest video game in history chose human labour to preserve the integrity of the game," Rose added.
Rose did raise some concerns about pay, though.

"Despite being paid well for my time on set, I'll never see a residual check for my work," Rose wrote, explaining that this is part of SAG’s contract with game developers. As a union leader at one of SAG's sister unions, Rose said there's still "a long way to go to ensure arts workers are fairly compensated for our labour".

Rose also says many other trans people worked on GTA 6, both in front of the camera and behind it. "SO many trans people besides me are featured in GTA VI as other roles, designers, writers, etc... take a note, theatre and TV! We are employable & profitable!!!"

Finally, Rose voiced support for Rockstar's UK staff. "UK-based workers at Rockstar Games are currently voting on whether to unionise, and I sincerely hope their efforts are successful," Rose wrote. "Every arts worker should have a stable job with benefits and fair working conditions protected by a union."

GTA 6 is out now on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It launched on Thursday, although some have been getting in on the action earlier, as a whopping 2m Xbox players in the UK and US took advantage of the trick of changing their console's country. Even New Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty. "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first."

Eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

articles.headline: I spent two weeks with Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, and it’s a stellar all-rounder with a gorgeous nanomatte display — but it needs a clearer reason to be
keyFacts: Amazon launched the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, a new Android-based device starting at $499 that replaces the company's older FireOS platform.
TechRadar stated that the optional nanomatte screen upgrade is a major highlight, providing excellent anti-glare performance for its price point.
The reviewer noted drawbacks including middling hardware specs, flat speakers, heavy weight, and expensive optional keyboard and stylus accessories.
body: TechRadar Verdict

On paper, Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 12 Pro might not seem terribly exciting; most specs are middling, Alexa’s inclusion is far from a selling point and, based on Amazon’s track record, the company’s services can do more to interrupt a product’s usefulness than inform it. However, between its gorgeous nanomatte screen, stylish design, and clever features (especially for Kindle fans), the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is a surprisingly exciting device and a solid start for Amazon’s post-FireOS era.
Reasons to buy
- + Finally, FireOS is laid to rest
- + Nanomatte display is among the best screens at its price
- + Svelte and functional design, barring weight
- + Great for reading, good for entertainment
Reasons to avoid
- - Specs might not offer longevity
- - Expensive peripherals
- - Not entirely clear of Amazon bloat
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: One-minute review

When Amazon announced its new Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, I found myself at a crossroads. On the one hand, despite my criticisms of the company’s product ecosystem, I’ve used Amazon Echo smart speakers and displays to control my smart home for several years, and I do appreciate the brand’s approach to providing a broad spectrum of price points in its device lineup.

But I don’t like that many of these devices are treated as billboards for Amazon’s wider products and services, and Kindle Fire tablets are (or were) the biggest offenders; FireOS was a sluggish, bloatware-loaded platform that barely functioned in itself, let alone as a tablet OS with its limited app store.

So, hearing that Amazon had launched an Android-based tablet came as a genuinely welcome surprise, and I was particularly excited to try its top-of-the-line 12-inch nanomatte screen model. I’ve spent two weeks testing the Alexa Tab 12 Pro, and while it’s still far from perfect, it’s a surprisingly competent and well-thought-out device for the price. With time (and perhaps a second-generation model), Amazon could finally be making its mark in the tablet market.

The Tab 12 Pro’s design is simple but slick, its specs are decent enough and help keep the price low, and some of the added features (including those that drive the user towards Amazon services) feel smartly integrated into the tablet. And the nanomatte display variant? It’s a triumph for Amazon: clear and crisp, defiant to most reflections unless under direct light and wonderfully vibrant.

I’ve not seen the non-nanomatte version of the Alexa Tab 12 Pro, but I can’t imagine it lives up to the model I tested; in all likelihood, nanomatte is every bit worth the $50/£50 upgrade. Equipped with it, the Tab 12 Pro’s 12-inch display is one of the best screens in its category, and really, that’s what a lot of everyday customers are looking for versus performant chipsets, high-spec cameras, and powerful speakers.

That being said, the cracks do show in some of the Tab 12 Pro’s lower-end specs, and it feels a little like Amazon’s focus on delivering a well-rounded product comes at the expense of the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro having a real, hard-hitting selling point — and perhaps its longevity, too.

For instance, while its blue light-reducing reading profiles, 3:2 aspect ratio, paperlike screen texture, and slick Kindle experience make it great for reading books and documents alike, it’s too heavy to use one-handed and stash away like a typical e-reader. For streaming video, the screen is bright and clear, but that vibrancy I mentioned before can mean colors are a little overblown, even if you tune them down with the different profiles in settings, and the tablet’s speakers are pretty flat if you want to listen aloud.

This is a thread that will follow through much of my commentary on Amazon’s best-ever tablet; being a ‘jack of all trades, master of none’ device doesn’t really do much for me, even in a general-use tablet. Still, the Alexa Tab 12 Pro is far from a disappointment overall, and especially for Prime members, Kindle lovers, or those wanting a great household management-come-productivity slate, it’s a really solid Android tablet.
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Price & availability
- Starts at $499/£449 for the 12-inch model without nanomatte
- Alexa Tablet Pro keyboard is $149.99 / £129.99
- Alexa Tablet Pro Pen is $89.99 / £79.99
- Available at Amazon

The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro comes in at $499/£449 in its base configuration with 128GB storage and its standard display; for $/£50 more you can add the nanomatte display, and for $/£100 more you can upgrade to 16GB RAM / 256GB storage.

There are optional peripherals to factor in too; sold separately, the keyboard costs $149.99 / £129.99, and the stylus is $89.99 / £79.99, but you can bundle these in with the tablet for an added cost of $150/£140. These are fairly steep standalone prices, so if you think there’s a chance you’ll benefit from these peripherals, I’d buy them outright.

While a lot of the Tablet 12 Pro’s specs are middling, at its price point and versus the competition, this is a pretty solid value proposition; Amazon will often trim the fat from its hardware to reach low prices, and it’s a similar story across the other smaller tablets in this lineup. The Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $229.99 / £199.99 with 4GB RAM and 64GB storage, and the Tablet 11 comes in at $329.99 / £289.99 with 8GB RAM and 64GB storage.

By comparison, Samsung’s Galaxy Tab S10 FE is slightly less powerful, has a slightly smaller battery and a 90Hz screen, but does offer a slightly better front camera; it starts at $549.99 / £539. Apple’s latest iPad Air comes in at $749 / £749, and while it does offer the more powerful M4 chipset, it’s smaller at 11 inches and has a static 60Hz display versus the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro’s 120Hz.

I’ve seen a lot of discussion around whether the Tablet 12 Pro’s low price is worth paying for a product that will inevitably become more of an ad platform as new updates roll out. With the freedom of Android OS, it’s a little easier for consumers to have their say on what they see by downloading a different launcher, but I’d be doing a disservice to those who have been burned by aggressively targeted ads (especially on the Echo Show) if I didn’t at least acknowledge how ads may factor into the value proposition here. That being said, I’ve barely seen anything ads-wise in my time testing the Tablet 12 Pro…
- Value score: 4/5
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Specs
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Design
- Slick and simple design
- A little on the heavier side
- Magnetic peripherals (added cost) for productivity
Amazon’s not changing the game with its Alexa Tablet design aesthetically, but there are a few things of note about its slate.

Its 3:2 aspect ratio (270.8 mm x 183.85 mm x 6.5 mm) makes it a great tablet for productivity; you can read documents and books with ease, and there’s plenty of room for multitasking in its horizontal orientation. It’s a little heavy at 550g, but it does feel well-built, offering IP52 dust and splash resistance. There’s an elegance here I’m not quite used to in Amazon’s products; from the cursive Alexa branding on the back panel to the premium-feeling aluminum casing, which is surprisingly smudge-proof.

Embedded into the right-hand side bezel, the 8MP front camera is positioned just off-center when the tablet is stationed horizontally, and on the rear of the tablet, there’s a 13MP main camera — both offer 1080p full HD video.

On the right side of the tablet’stop edge, there’s a fingerprint sensor lock button, and at the top of its right-hand side is the volume rocker. On the bottom edge, you’ll find its USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 port (the smaller screen models have USB-C 2.0, for what it’s worth) and along the left-hand side are four pogo pins for attaching the folio keyboard.

Speaking of which, Amazon sent me the keyboard casing and stylus to test for this review, and while the price to add them both is a little steep, they unlock a great deal of functionality in the tablet. I wish Amazon had added a backlight at this price point, but broadly speaking, I’ve very few complaints.

The chiclet keyboard is soft and clicky but sturdy, featuring a dedicated Alexa+ key in lieu of a right control button as well as a writing assist key in the top-right hand corner. The trackpad is responsive and smooth, and there are ample shortcuts for productivity users. I don’t love the magnetically attaching rear cover and its fold-out kickstand; a few too many times, this popped off of the tablet while I was adjusting the height, and it doesn’t offer much stability if you want to use the tablet on your lap, or indeed any uneven surface.

The stylus magnetically attaches and charges, and offers a nice weight for a natural drawing experience. Its top end can be used as an eraser, and if it’s missing, you can find it by triggering an admittedly soft and quiet ping.
- Design score: 4/5
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Display
- Optional nanomatte display is well worth the upgrade
- Smooth and super responsive
- Great features for reading
The finest feather in the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro’s cap is its main screen, an opinion which is colored, by and large, by my love for the optional nanomatte display.

The tablet’s 12-inch 2.8K LCD screen offers a 2800 x 1840 resolution, 280ppi (pixels per inch), and a buttery smooth 120Hz touchscreen. I’ve only seen and tested the nanomatte version, and that’s a real boon when it comes to anti-glare; in every circumstance barring direct sunlight or direct indoor light like nearby table lamps, it’s easy to see from most viewing angles, even despite only offering 500 nits of brightness.

The default color profile is Boosted; I found this to be a bit too vibrant in most settings, in particular while watching TV series, but the Natural profile is much better unless you’re in an especially bright environment.

The gritty, paper-like nanomatte texture makes it easy on the eyes when reading, too — and even offers a decent bite for drawing and writing with the Alexa Tablet Pro Pen. That being said, I noticed there’s poor palm detection while drawing in apps like Clip Studio Paint, so if you’re looking for the best possible tablet for drawing, you’re better off with more specialized slates like the iPad Pro or Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 Ultra.
- Display score: 4.5/5
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Performance
- Yay for Android…
- But app compatibility issues and remnants of Amazon bloatware remain
- Makes the most out of some middling specs

Unlock the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, and you’re greeted by its default launcher with Amazon services and Alexa baked in; these elements are omnipresent, with a widget in the top-left corner for recently viewed media on Amazon platforms as well as the Ask Alexa search bar in the bottom-right corner, which pops out into a chat window when pressed.

I don’t hate these features as much as other reviewers and customers seem to, but that’s in part because I often do want to hop back into my last-read Kindle book or quickly dive back into playlists, movies and TV series. And besides that, the Tablet 12 Pro is far less egregious with its advertising (at least, for now) than other Amazon devices I’ve used. Plus, thanks to Android OS, you can just switch out to another launcher if you really hate Amazon’s footprint.

As well as Amazon's own apps, Google takes up a fair amount of real estate by default, with its own app folder as well as a Google search bar in the top right corner. Swipe left, and you land in the content center with recommended content from Prime, Kindle, and Luna, and swipe up for your app tray; all fairly standard for Android tablets overall.

The Kindle experience is a particular highlight. When you open books in the app, the screen will automatically toggle into reading mode, which reduces blue-light emission, silences distractions like notifications, and extends the battery life. Were the tablet a little lighter and more portable, I’d say it’s a great replacement for Kindle users who want more than just e-reading, but I wouldn’t personally stash this in my backpack to read while on the go quite as readily as I would Amazon’s latest thin-and-light e-readers. What’s more, most of these features are exclusive to the Kindle app.

As an entertainment hub, the Tab 12 Pro is decent enough; the 3:2 aspect ratio isn’t ideal, as you do see quite a bit of letterboxing while streaming content, and the sound quality from the built-in speakers is a little tinny and bassless.

The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is no powerhouse; it’s middling at best, but at its price and for vast swathes of its target market, that’s perfectly fine. Its MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor is perfectly capable for light multitasking, moderately demanding apps and some AI tasks, but don’t expect iPad Pro- or Samsung Galaxy S10 Ultra-grade speeds here.

Still, the Tablet 12 Pro is a very capable productivity machine, whether in split-screen or desktop mode, and especially with its peripherals in tow. I played games like Wuthering Waves and used Clip Studio Paint and, broadly speaking, performance was fine in both applications – even in desktop mode with a hefty update running in the background for Wuthering Waves, YouTube playing in windowed mode and typing on GDocs, the tablet handled the load pretty well, though it did get a little warm in the process.

In my time with the Tab 12 Pro, I also encountered some stuttering when switching between apps, a few crashes, and some software lag, which could be any combination of the less powerful chipset and Amazon’s software. This, plus the long-running woes of Android app compatibility limiting the library of optimized apps, can cause friction in use.
Generally speaking, though, the Tab 12 Pro is pretty capable. I’m not convinced that will be the case in 3-4 years, which does give me pause, but only time will tell how these specs hold up.
Other features
Battery

I struggle a little with Amazon’s promise of 16 hours of video playback; just 4 hours of streaming Netflix series wiped out 50% of my battery life, and I was completely out after 8 hours. Combined with the tablet’s 2-3 hour recharge time, this isn’t ideal, but it will still last you throughout the workday so long as you’re not running lots of power-hungry apps at once without turning on power-saving mode.
Alexa and AI services

Alexa has the same issues here as it does across Amazon’s platforms; namely, that it’s built more as a shopping assistant than anything else. For smart home control, timer setting, and simple requests, it’s broadly fine, and you can download third-party assistants if you want more demanding tasks completed. You can access Gemini’s writing tools natively from the keyboard peripheral, too.
Cameras

Far from being standout features, the tablet’s cameras are decent enough; the 8MP front camera is good enough for video calls, and the 13MP rear camera is fine for shooting a quick photo or video in a pinch, albeit the results will be quite saturated. This is far from a deal-breaker in a general-use tablet, but if you like a crisp video feed for business calls, you’re better off with a more pro-grade slate.
- Performance score: 3.5/5
Should I buy the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro?
Buy it if…
You use a lot of Amazon services
If you’re a Prime subscriber who uses Kindle services, Prime Video and/or Luna, this is a great companion to fit into your wider Amazon device ecosystem.
You want a solid productivity tablet without a high price tag
At its price, this is a competitive productivity slate, even with the added cost of peripherals, and it’s capable of moderate loads as well as multitasking.
You do a lot of reading

With its nanomatte coating in particular, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is great for reading in and out of its optimized Kindle experience. The 3:2 aspect ratio lends itself to documents and books in both horizontal and vertical orientation, and the screen is very easy on the eyes.
Don’t buy it if…
You don’t like Amazon services

Yes, you can switch to a different launcher, but at its core, this is an Alexa-first package. It’s in the name, and though there are limited ways Amazon can mess with Android’s open design philosophy, you might prefer something that’s less Amazon-y out of the box.
You want an entertainment hub before all else
Streaming is fine on the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, but its aspect ratio isn’t optimal for TVs and movies, and the speakers are middling at best.
Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Also consider
Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE

It’s comparable in terms of specs and price; while it has a slightly less powerful chipset and a slightly smaller 90Hz screen, it does have better IP68 water and dust resistance, 45W fast charging, and comes with the S Pen included. Plus, it’s less Amazon-y.
Apple iPad Air

The smaller, 11-inch iPad Air is certainly more powerful than the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro thanks to Apple’s M4 chip, but it has a static 60Hz 264ppi display and, of course, runs iPadOS rather than Android.
How I tested the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro
- I used the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro for two weeks
- I used it as a productivity device as well as an entertainment device
- I benchmarked against mid-range tablets

During my two weeks with the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, I used it to write much of this review while exporting files and using various productivity apps, as well as for gaming and streaming content and using apps like Clip Studio Paint to test the drawing experience. I tried its advertised features, including desktop mode and split-screen, the built-in Alexa chat function, and Amazon app experiences like Kindle.

I benchmarked the device against comparable mid-range tablets like the Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE and the iPad Air (M4), playing demanding games like Wuthering Waves and completing multitasking workloads to see how it performs under pressure. I ran the battery down to 0% while streaming content on Netflix and recharged the device fully to measure battery performance.
I’m a regular iPad Pro user and have tested a variety of mobile computing devices in my five years at TechRadar, including Android slates, drawing tablets and beyond.

articles.headline: Nine OPTA Stats that will get Leeds fans excited ahead of Chelsea clash
keyFacts: Leeds United sits ninth in the Premier League table with 14 points after 10 matches ahead of their clash against Chelsea.
Leeds holds one of the league's best defensive records, conceding only eight goals, and leads the division in high-intensity pressures.
Leeds forward Noah Okafor ranks among the Premier League's most clinical finishers with a goal every 112 minutes since February.
body: Nine OPTA Stats that will get Leeds fans excited ahead of Chelsea clash Daniel Farke's side return to Premier League action looking to build on their impressive 1-0 victory over Tottenham Hotspur before the international break, with the Whites facing another big test against Xabi Alonso's Chelsea.

Leeds have made an encouraging start to the campaign, sitting ninth in the table after 10 matches, and the latest statistics from our friends at OPTA Stats highlight several reasons for the Whites to be confident heading to the capital.
Here are nine facts to know ahead of the contest.
1. Leeds boast one of the Premier League's best defensive records
Only Arsenal and Brighton have conceded fewer Premier League goals than Leeds United this season.
The Whites have shipped just eight goals in their opening 10 fixtures, underlining the defensive improvements made by Farke's side and providing a solid platform to build upon.
2. James Trafford is leading the way between the posts
Leeds goalkeeper James Trafford has made the second-most saves in the Premier League this season, with 37 from his opening 10 appearances.
The shot-stopper has been a key figure for the Whites, producing a series of important interventions to help his side maintain one of the division's strongest defensive records.
3. Nobody presses quite like Leeds United
Farke's side have applied more high-intensity pressures in the opposition half than any other Premier League team this season.
Leeds have registered 1,701 such pressures, while 47.8 per cent of their opponents' touches in the opposition half have been met with a high-intensity press. Both figures rank first in the division.
It highlights the energy, intensity and collective work rate that have become important features of the Whites' approach.
4. Leeds are the Premier League's leading set-piece threat
The Whites have generated more expected goals from set-pieces, excluding penalties, than any other team in the Premier League this season.
Their total stands at 6.1 xG, with set-pieces proving an increasingly important attacking weapon for Farke's side.
Indeed, Leeds' only two goals across their last four league matches have both come from dead-ball situations, with a throw-in and a corner providing the breakthroughs.
5. Chelsea could be vulnerable from set-pieces

There is an interesting opportunity for Leeds to exploit at Stamford Bridge, with Chelsea having conceded eight goals from set-pieces in the big five European leagues this season, excluding penalties.
Only Italian side Monza, with nine, have conceded more.
With Leeds already demonstrating their effectiveness from these situations, it could be an important area of Saturday's encounter.
6. Noah Okafor is among the Premier League's most clinical finishers
Only one player has a better minutes-per-goal ratio than Leeds forward Noah Okafor among Premier League players to have featured for at least 500 minutes since the start of February.
The Swiss international has scored eight goals in 894 minutes of action during that period, averaging a goal every 112 minutes.
Only Benjamin Sesko, who has scored once every 83 minutes, boasts a better return.
7. Leeds enjoyed the better of last season's meetings
The Whites avoided defeat in both Premier League meetings with Chelsea during the 2025/26 campaign.
Leeds claimed an impressive 3-1 victory at Elland Road before earning a hard-fought 2-2 draw at Stamford Bridge.
The Whites will be hoping to continue that positive record against the Blues this weekend, having last gone unbeaten in three consecutive meetings between November 2000 and October 2001.
8. Noah Okafor has a habit of delivering decisive moments
Okafor's goals have proved particularly valuable for Leeds, with four of his last eight Premier League strikes for the club being match-winners.
Furthermore, the Whites have lost just one of the nine Premier League matches in which the forward has found the net, recording seven victories and one draw.
The attacker was once again on target in Leeds' most recent outing, scoring the decisive goal in the 1-0 victory over Tottenham Hotspur at Elland Road.
9. Leeds have already shown they can compete with the best
The Whites head into the weekend sitting ninth in the Premier League table, having collected 14 points from their opening 10 fixtures.
With just two defeats across those matches, Farke's side have demonstrated their ability to compete consistently in the top flight.
Chelsea currently occupy fifth position with 16 points, meaning just two points separate the sides ahead of Saturday's meeting.
With Leeds having already beaten Tottenham and Newcastle United this season, the Whites will travel to Stamford Bridge determined to produce another statement performance.

articles.headline: Manchester City v Fulham: Premier League – live
keyFacts: Manchester City hosted Fulham at the Etihad Stadium seeking to end a run of three consecutive Premier League defeats.
Rodrigo Muniz scored the opening goal for Fulham in the first half after receiving an assist from Oscar Bobb.
Calvin Bassey received a yellow card for a foul on Phil Foden, who was marking the ninth anniversary of his Manchester City debut.
body: 23 min: Jeremy Doku tries to pick out Iliman Ndiaye with a lofted diagonal pass to the byline but overhits his delivery. The Senegal international is unable to prevent the ball from going out of play.
22 min: Calvin Bassey gets booked for a foul on Phil Foden, who is marking the ninth anniversary of his Manchester City debut. Nine years, eh? Where does the time go?

20 min: It was, to be fair, a fine finish from Muniz, who took a touch and curled an unstoppable effort past Donnarumma after Elliot Anderson and Ruben Dias had ushered Oscar Bobb through to provide the assist.

18 min: City have received a lot of criticism for conceding cheap goals in recent games and that’s another one to add to the list. A back-to-front effort in which both Bobb and Muniz went completely unchallenged as the visitors carved their way through the City bystanders.

And there it is! From a throw-in deep inside their own half, Fulham advance down the right with Oscar Bobb on the ball. He cuts inside and plays the ball to Rodrigo Muniz, who opens his body and curls a shot high past Gianluigi Donnarumma.
15 min: It’s been a fairly sedate return for the Premier League thus far and the crowd at the Etihad Stadium seem half-asleep. This game needs a goal to perk them up.
12 min: Ayyoub Bouaddi wins the ball from Kenny Tete in midfield and sends Manchester City on their weay upfield. Fulham don’t take long to win the ball back as Jeremy Doku runs into traffic.

8 min: Jeremy Doku sends a cross to the far post, Erling Haaland heads the ball back across the face of goal and David Affengruber leaps highest to nod the ball away from danger. Moments previously, the Fulham defender had done well to block an Erling Haaland shot.

6 min:Manchester City play the ball hither and yon inside their defensive third, trying to play their way through the Fulham press. There’s an early yellow card for Iwobi, who is booked for holding Elliot Anderson as the City midfielder tried to spin him.
4 min: A Sander Berge cross from the byline is put out for as Fulham corner following a mix-up between Iliman Ndiaye and Ruben Dias. Donnarumma fields the inswinger from Alex Iwobi.
3 min: Now Bernd Leno gets on the ball, lumping it long towards Rodrigo Muniz. The ball’s played wide to Kenny Tete, whose cross from the right is plucked from the air by Donnarumma.
2 min: A goalkeeper under a little bit of pressure after some recent ricks, Gianluigi Donnarumma gets a couple of early touches, fielding two back-passes with a minimum of fuss.

Not long now: Led by referee Tom Bramall and his team of match officials, both sets of players click-clack out on to the Etihad Stadium pitchon a crisp November afternoon in Manchester. They receive a guard of honour from an array of “Once A Blue” Manchester City legends including Mick McCarthy, Peter Barnes, Paul Lake and Davids White and Brightwell.

Enzo Maresca: The Manchester City boss was asked about the balance – or lack thereof – between attack and defence in his side during his audience with the press yesterday. “The same midfield that won seven games in a row is the same that lost three games in a row,” he said. “It’s football. The idea is to continue to attack in the same way, creating chances, but trying to create a balance when we defend. Sometimes we need more balance and different kind of players on the pitch. We are going to find solutions for a more balanced defensive back line and midfield.

“I was not thinking we were doing everything well when we were winning games. I’m not thinking we did everything wrong when we lost games. There are things we need to do better and no doubt we will do better. We are conceding too many goals. Most of them are avoidable. So we need to avoid mistakes and try to deal with it [better] when it happens.”

Manchester City: Will Unwin is at the Etihad Stadium for the Guardian and has filed this scene-setter from his place in the press box. “Without going over the top, it feels like a big day for Enzo Maresca,” he says. “After three Premier League defeats in a row, the Italian has to find improvement in his team. To do so, a change in midfield sees Ayyoub Bouaddi brought in to bring additional calmness alongside the all-action Elliot Anderson. With all the uncertainty swirling around this half of Manchester, getting matters on the pitch back on track is imperative. A statement win to prove there is full focus among the squad would be ideal but any will do against Fulham.”

Alvaro Arbeloa: “I have watched all Manchester City games and the last three games that they lost I woudn’t say they were the worst team,” said Fulham’s head coach in yesterday’s press conference. “They have the chances. You can see the quality of the players, how they want to play. They are very, very aggressive when they lose the ball, so for me they are performing really, really well.
“This is the Premier League, so you can feel how difficult every game is, but they won the first seven games, it was amazing. For me, they’re still one of the best teams in the world.”

Asked about speculation linking Fulham defender Calvin Bassey with a move to Manchester United, Alvaro stressed the Nigerian international’s importance to the Cottagers. “He’s very, very important,” he said. “He is one of my captains. From the first days when I arrived I saw how good he is. I think he is one of the best centre backs in the world, so it’s normal if there are so many teams that wants Calvin, that for me is normal.
“I’m not worried about that because I am really happy with Calvin. I think Calvin is really happy here. He is so important for us. He is one of our leaders.”

Elsewhere in Manchester: Maine Road FC,who play in English football’s tenth tier, aim to become a new home for any Manchester City supporters disillusioned by the possible consequences of the guilty verdict handed down to their team, and those priced out of the Premier League. Dominic Booth reports …

Gonzalo Garica: The Fulham striker and great nephew of Rita Hayworth admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he will remain calm over his 11-match goal drought. Interview: Sid Lowe.

Those teams: Enzo Maresca makes three changes to the City team that started against Nottingham Forest last time out, with Nico O’Reilly, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Phil Foden coming into his side. Josko Gvardiol, Enzo Fernandez and Rayan Cherki drop to the bench. Abdukodir Khusanov and Marc Guehi have both been selected despite missing out on international duty with Uzbekistan and England resepectively through injury.

There are also three changes to the Fulham side that lined up against Newcastle before the international break. Kenny Tete, Ryan Sessegnon and Rodrigo Muniz have been selected today, with Timothy Castagne, Antonee Robinson and Gonzalo Garcia making way.

Manchester City winger Antoine Semenyo remains sidelined with the knee injury he suffered against Ipswich in October, while defenders Marc Guehi and Abdukodir Khushanov have been rated doubtful for today’s game.

Speaking at his press conference yesterday, Fulham head coach Alvaro Arbeloa confirmed that reserve goalkeeper Benjamin Lecomte will be out for the season after rupturing his achillles tendon in a practice match played against West Ham behind closed doors during the international break.
Midfielder Tom Cairney is struggling with a knee injury but could feature in today’s squad, while Emile Smith-Rowe is unlikely to be in the matchday squad as he has a hip injury.

Following the second international break of the season, the Premier League resumes at the Etihad Stadium, with Manchester City hoping to halt a run of three consecutive defeats in the top flight. The most recent came against Nottingham Forest at the City Ground, where Liam Delap scored two quite extraordinary goals against the club where he learnt his trade.

Fulham are unbeaten in four matches and came from behind to draw with Newcastle at Craven Cottage last time out. Rather astonishingly, they haven’t beaten Manchester City since 2009 and have lost 20 consecutive games against today’s hosts in an extraordinary run of defeats against the same opponents dating back to 2012. Kick-off at the Etihad Stadium is at 12.30pm (GMT) but we’ll have team news and buildup in the meantime.

articles.headline: NFL players allowed to use Viagra to help rise to Mexico altitude – six-time Pro Bowler took it before every game
keyFacts: NFL players are permitted to use Viagra to combat the effects of high altitude during a game in Mexico.
The medication widens blood vessels in the lungs, helping athletes maintain stamina and reduce fatigue caused by thinner air.
Former NFL player Chad Johnson previously revealed on social media that he took Viagra before games to boost his performance.
body: NFL players looking to boost their performance in the Mexican altitude would be allowed to use Viagra.
The Minnesota Vikings and San Francisco 49ers have travelled to Mexico for their Week 11 clash, with the NFL returning to Mexico for the first time since 2022.
The NFL is headed back to Mexico for the first time since 2022 Getty

But the playing conditions will be difficult for all involved due to the altitude, with the 87,500-capacity Estadio Azteca – one of the most iconic soccer/football venues in the world – situated 7,720 feet (approximately 2,240 meters) above sea level.
Take the 2026 World Cup for example, when England players felt the full wrath of the conditions in a 3-2 win over Mexico in what was arguably one of the games of the tournament.

The use of sildenafil – which is more commonly known as Viagra – is not on the NFL’s list of prohibited substances, nor is it on the latest list of banned substances by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA).

As such, some of the league’s biggest names like Brock Purdy , Christian McCaffrey , Kirk Cousins , and Justin Jefferson are all permitted to use it should they wish to, although there has been no suggestion that any of them will.
Benefits of taking Viagra at high altitude
So what is it about the prescription medication that is so beneficial in high altitude?
Well, in the modern day it is most commonly used to treat erectile dysfunction, but it was initially developed to serve as a treatment for high blood pressure.
The way it works is that it widens the blood vessels in the lungs after blocking an enzyme that restricts them.
This is crucial at high altitudes due to the thinner atmosphere and lower concentration of oxygen available making it much harder for the heart to pump blood containing oxygen around the body.
Essentially, without it, it would be difficult for even the fittest of athletes to maintain the stamina they would exude on any other day, which could lead to earlier fatigue and dizziness.
Therefore, the use of Viagra would help counteract these feelings caused by high altitudes due to its ability to reduce the blood pressure in the lungs.
49ers stars like McCaffrey and Kittle could be considering taking Viagra before they take to the field at the Azteca Getty
The 49ers were participants in the last time the NFL staged a game in Mexico Getty
Have NFL players used Viagra in the past?
Some players have been very vocal in the past about going the extra mile to get an advantage – legally, of course – over some stiff (pardon the pun) competition.
Legendary wide receiver Chad Johnson is one of those, revealing back in July 2020 that he would take Viagra before games in an effort to boost his performance.
“I took viagra before every game & people thought they’d stop me, if my stat line was bad i wasn’t covered, the pass was just incomplete,” he tweeted on X in July 2020.
When a fan asked why he took it, in which he posted, “NFL tests for steroids, how you gone stop me running on 3 legs every Sunday, no hat.”
These tweets resurfaced over a year later and Johnson, who once legally changed his name to Chad Ochocinco in reference to his No. 85 jersey, doubled down on taking the substance.

He wrote: “I was dead serious, I’d take viagra then a muscle relaxer before each game, the increase in blood flow throughout the body wouldn’t allow me to get tired & i could run for 8 quarters if need be, no hat.”
The Vikings could consider taking Viagra to gain an edge in Mexico Getty
Former Bengals star Chad Johnson revealed in 2020 he used to take Viagra before games to reduce fatigue and increase bloodflow Getty

Former wide receiver Brandon Marshall once alluded to fellow players taking Viagra back in 2012 when he was playing for the Chicago Bears , although he admitted it was a “scary” thought due to concerns over the chemicals that can be in these types of substances.
In 2015, research was conducted into the athletic benefits of Viagra, which found an improved ‘ exercise performance at high altitude (>3,800 m) in a subset of athletes by greater than 35 per cent’.

At the end of the day, though, attitude trumps altitude and the match-up between two of the very best teams in the NFL this season should provide enthralling entertainment, whether their players decide to take the hard stuff or not.

articles.headline: Germany's religious freedom report: Authoritarian regimes, holy wars, and spies abroad
keyFacts: A new German government report states that global freedom of religion and belief deteriorated between 2023 and 2025.
The report examines restrictions in 30 countries and warns against transnational repression operating inside Germany.
Religious freedom commissioner Thomas Rachel expressed hope that parliamentary committees will discuss the report.
body: The report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," said Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Recently adopted by the Cabinet, the government's fourth report on the subject covers developments from 2023 to 2025.

The government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world. According to the report, this freedom is facing "increasing pressure" globally. The focus is not primarily on the suppression of religious institutions or structures, but on the situation of individuals who hold a religious belief, or none at all.
Authoritarian regimes increase pressure on religious communities

The importance of religious freedom is reflected in the way the government commissioner describes the issue: "Religion and faith are of great importance to four out of five people around the world and are central to their identity. People wake up with God and go to sleep with God. It is part of their everyday lives." Research by the Pew Research Center suggests that about 84% of the world's population identifies with a certain religion.

At a time when authoritarian regimes are gaining ground and expanding their surveillance capabilities, the report paints a bleak picture. The growing number of violent conflicts, the rise of authoritarian rule, and the spread of populism have led to "painful restrictions on freedom of religion and belief around the world."

The German government report does not attempt to provide a statistical tally of attacks or the number of people facing persecution. Instead, it examines 30 countries as case studies where, in the federal government's view, freedom of religion and belief is being restricted. These include about six countries each from Africa, Asia, and the Arab world. In Europe, the report focuses on Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Turkey, while in Latin America it highlights Mexico, Nicaragua, and Cuba. It also identifies shortcomings in five of the world's six most populous countries: China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Nigeria.

Regarding India, the report refers to "Hindu nationalist efforts" that threaten the equal treatment of all officially recognized religions. It states that the generally peaceful coexistence of different faiths is "repeatedly overshadowed by tensions and, at times, violence." Both Muslim and Christian communities report growing intolerance and hate speech. According to the report, violent Hindu extremist groups have carried out a "large number of physical attacks" against Muslims, while the police and government authorities often respond inadequately.

In China, the German government identifies a "significant tightening of the legal framework of state control at the expense of freedom of religion and belief." According to the report, this particularly affects Uyghurs, Tibetans, and churches that lack official state approval and are subject to harsh measures by the authorities. The law on the "Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress," which came into force on July 1, 2026, subordinates religion to "the formation of national identity" and patriotic education.

One of the countries where the situation has deteriorated most dramatically is Nicaragua, which has severely restricted freedom of religion and belief since 2018. The repression has primarily targeted the Catholic Church. According to the report, "intimidation, persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion" have forced around 130 priests and nuns to leave the country.

The reports reserves some of its sharpest criticism for Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church. Under his leadership, the church has strongly supported Russia's war against Ukraine and portrayed it as a "holy war." According to the report, "weapons are blessed, Russian soldiers are absolved of their sins, and donations are collected for the war." It is perhaps the clearest example in the report of how religion can be used to justify oppression and violence.
Intimidation reaches beyond borders

The report explicitly addresses the threat posed by "transnational repression" (TNR), which it describes as a "growing global problem" that also affects Germany. The term refers to the persecution or intimidation of individuals by their country of origin beyond its own borders.

Ultimately, it argues, this amounts to a "continuation of domestic repression." Such "cross-border repression" has become considerably easier through the growing availability of digital means of repression, including smear campaigns on social media and spyware.

These forms of pressure range from physical attacks on individuals to digital assaults such as online intimidation and defamation. In some cases, repression is also carried out by threatening family members who remain in the country of origin. Russia and Iran, for example, are identified as the "main perpetrators of transnational repression" in Germany.

China is a particularly prominent example of religious and ideological tensions. Repression by Beijing in Germany primarily targets members of groups that the country's Communist Party classifies as "hostile to the system." These include Uyghurs, Tibetans, and members of the Falun Gong movement. According to the report, they are "also subject to surveillance and repressive measures in Germany," while relatives living in China are pressured.

Thomas Rachel hopes the newly published report will be "discussed in as many Bundestag committees as possible" and that members of parliament will "engage with the issue accordingly." Previous government reports on the subject have been debated in the Bundestag plenary at least once and, in some cases, twice.
Religion: A matter of German foreign policy

The issue's place within the German government has also changed during the current legislative term. Commissioner Thomas Rachel is now based at the Foreign Ministry, while both of his predecessors since 2018 were attached to the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. Today, Rachel says, the importance of religion is being "taken into account" in German foreign policy. He also points to his involvement in the Foreign Ministry's diplomatic training programs.

In doing so, the government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) reversed a structural decision made by the previous center-left coalition, which was led from 2021 to 2025 by Chancellor Olaf Scholz of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The Scholz government had reduced the issue's prominence by assigning it to the "Religion and Foreign Policy" division. Religion and foreign policy have now regained a more prominent place within government.

One example is the current foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, who has already visited the Vatican more often than his two predecessors combined. In addition, alongside Rachel, the ministry has for some time maintained a dedicated unit headed by an ambassador that deals with, among other things, "fundamental issues relating to religion and foreign policy."

articles.headline: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
keyFacts: Anthropic staff member Levent Alpöge claimed he solved the Riemann Hypothesis math problem using the company's AI tool, Claude.

body: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.

Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.

Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.

A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.

Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.

"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.
He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.

"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."

Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.

"This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," he said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."
Alpöge said he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics." He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.
In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.

"Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis," said Kontorovich. "There's some kind of out-of-body experience where I'm looking at myself saying, 'Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,' and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth."
Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.

Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI's future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.

articles.headline: Engadget review recap: Apple HomeView, Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) and more
keyFacts: Engadget published a roundup of 14 product reviews completed over two weeks, covering tech from Apple, Meta, Microsoft, and others.
Engadget reported that Apple's new HomeView smart display has category-leading sound, but relies heavily on iPhones and Siri AI.
Reporter Karissa Bell said Meta's Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 smart glasses are more expensive despite offering little more than their predecessor.
body: Engadget review recap: Apple HomeView, Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) and more
A roundup of recent reviews from Engadget.

14 reviews in 14 days. We've been busy. Before you start to wind down for the upcoming turkey-fueled feast, catch up on all of the reviews we've written over the last two weeks. There's a trio of new Apple products, two pairs of glasses, a bunch of gaming gear and more. We've collected everything here for easy reference, so read on to see what you might've missed.
Apple HomeView, Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2

All three of the main devices that Apple announced at its Welcome Home event hit my desk at the same time. I tackled the HomeView and fourth-gen Apple TV 4K first. Apple's debut smart display has a crisp, colorful screen and it's useful for the entire family. It features category-leading sound and a refined design. However, it's heavily reliant on your iPhone, and Siri AI still fails at fairly basic tasks. You'll also be at the mercy of thrid-party support, since the device runs CarPlay-enabled apps.

The new Apple TV 4K remains the best streaming box you can by. It's speedy and now has built-in mics for Siri. It's more expensive though, so it's not as easy to recommend as it was before. When it comes to the HomePod mini 2, that's not a device you should really be considering until it's outfitted with the new version of Siri AI. And there's no timeline for when that might happen.
Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) and Xreal Aura

It seems like Meta announces new smart glasses on a weekly basis these days. While the company isn't keeping quite that rapid of a pace, it did announce three models recently. One of those is the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3, the latest version of its "flagship" smart glasses. The cameras are still here, and the displays still aren't. But the new model is more expensive, and doesn't offer much more than its predecessor, according to senior reporter Karissa Bell.

The Xreal Aura is a set of Android XR glasses, but as Devindra found out, great hardware can't overcome the issues with Google's platform. "Xreal has delivered yet another light, bright and comfortable pair of AR specs with the Aura, but it's clearly hampered by a half-baked Android XR platform," he said. "Even worse, Android XR is a major reason why it costs twice as much as the company's previous hardware."
Surface Laptop Ultra

Devindra also put Microsoft's flagship RTX Spark laptop through its paces recently. The Surface Laptop Ultra is sleek and powerful, but it's also expensive, and it lags behind Apple's M5 Pro laptops in terms of performance. "The Surface Laptop Ultra's sheer refinement is a sign of just how far Microsoft has come," he said.
Everything else

Contributing reviews writer James Trew tested the HoverAir Versa. This gadget is a gimbal camera that transforms into a drone. Or is it a drone that doubles as a gimbal camera? Either way, the Versa has its benefits, but it doesn't particularly excel at either task.

If gaming is more your thing, UK bureau chief Mat Smith tested the highly-customizable Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited controller while senior reporter Jessica Conditt parked the Sony 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook (yes, that's really the name) on her desk for a few weeks. And if you prefer to do your gaming with a mouse, senior reporter Sam Rutherford test drove the SteelSeries Rival Pro.

Contributing reviews writer Tim Stevens went behind the wheel of the 2027 Chevy Bolt, lamenting that one of the best EVs won't be around for much longer. Sam also tried his best to lose his belongings to test out the new Pixel Tag, while senior reporter Daniel Cooper monitored his brain waves (and productivity) with the Neurable One headphones. And when that was done, he discovered how handy a seemingly mundane device can be with the Pebble Index 01 ring.

articles.headline: Australia's Chaudhary downs England in tetchy first T20
keyFacts: Australia defeated England by three wickets in the first T20 international in Melbourne after successfully chasing a target of 188.
Nikhil Chaudhary starred for Australia by taking two wickets for 21 runs and scoring 66 runs in a tense match.
England can level the five-match series when the teams play again in Gold Coast on Tuesday.
body: - Published
First T20, Melbourne Cricket Ground
England 187-9 (20 overs): Brook 65 (28), Banton 39 (22); Chaudhary 2-21
Australia 191-7 (19.5 overs): Chaudhary 66 (38)
Australia won by three wickets
Unlikely Australia international Nikhil Chaudhary rattled England and was the match-winner in a tense and tetchy final-over victory in the first T20 international in Melbourne.

Born in Delhi and a team-mate of India captain Shubman Gill in Indian domestic cricket, Chaudhary only switched to representing Australia after the Covid pandemic meant he got stuck in Brisbane celebrating his 24th birthday.

Progression through Australian club and domestic cricket followed - plus a stint working in a Mexican restaurant - before the 30-year-old played his standout performance to date in his fourth international at the Melbourne Cricket Ground.
Helping restrict England to 187-9 despite Harry Brook's fireworks in smashing 65 off 28 balls, Chaudhary took 2-21 with his mystery spin and then hit 66 to steer Australia within 20 runs of victory.
The elegant right-hander appeared to anger both Liam Dawson and Sam Curran during his knock and the MCG crowd loudly booed England as the tourists slowed the game in the final moments.
"You always know it is going to be a big game against England so there is going to be some chirp," said Chaudhary.

Curran was left with 11 to defend from the last over but all-rounder Jack Edwards finished with 25 not out as Australia completed their highest chase on home soil with three wickets and one ball remaining.
The win offers some relief to Australia - an XI featuring a host of new faces putting aside the ongoing sandpaper scandal to take a 1-0 lead in the five-match series.
England can level the contest in Gold Coast on Tuesday.
Chaudhary lets cricket do the talking
After all of the off-field issues that have overshadowed this tour, this was a welcome entertaining game of cricket.
England lost Phil Salt to the first ball of the match and afterwards there was boundary-hitting, comically bad fielding by Australia, a bit of needle and a grandstand finish.
Chaudhary should take the headlines. After opener Jake Fraser-McGurk fell in the first over and Mitchell Marsh was sluggish in making 37, he found scoring more straightforward.
He repeatedly targeted the off side and, after Australia lost 3-13 from 143-3, he pressed on the accelerator by hitting Will Jacks for six and Jamie Overton for two fours.
The incidents with Dawson and Curran appeared innocuous but words were exchanged. The umpire intervened in the Curran spat to encourage Chaudhary to continue his innings.
By hitting Overton to deep square-leg at the end of the 18th over, he allowed England back into the game.
However, Edwards kept his nerve, while England also had to deal with Jacks having to leave the field with a cut hand after four balls of the penultimate over.
Chaudhary once said he switched allegiance to Australia because he feels "more close to Australian culture than Indian culture".
Fittingly then, he experienced the wild cheers of an MCG crowd after the winning runs were hit.
"My parents came over from India last night," he said. "It is their first game watching me as well."
Brook knock in vain
When Brook had England 110-2 in the ninth over, the tourists looked on course for a score well over 200.
The four Australia wickets they took from the 16th over gave them a chance but it was their failure not to add another 15 or 20 runs earlier on that cost them.
England's skipper had a quiet ODI series with 23 runs across the three matches. Here he reaffirmed his position as one of the leading white-ball batters in the world.

He was dropped on two and three - both relatively straightforward chances among the six put down by Australia - but burst into life when hitting Riley Meredith for three consecutive sixes in the fourth over and was particularly destructive with his pull shot.
Brook's dismissal came when he tried to guide a cut off Chaudhary. Banton, who made 39 and shared a stand of 97 with Brook, followed in the next over and England never got going again.
After scoring 119 in the first 10 overs, they managed only 68 in the second, with Curran scoring 21 from 20, Jacks out for three and Jordan Cox never breaking free when making 27 from 20 balls.
With bowlers Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker now preparing for the Test series against South Africa, England need more from Curran and Jamie Overton, who took 1-37 and 1-44 respectively.

articles.headline: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
keyFacts: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called attacks on the Crimean Bridge a fair response to 109 Russian strikes on Ukrainian bridges.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting met Zelensky in Kyiv to demonstrate European unity and urge increased defense support for Ukraine.
Finland reinstated safety restrictions in the Gulf of Finland after detecting a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel.
body: - Published

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He also rejected the claim the Russian president made in China that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders met in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys to discuss Ukraine.
That meeting came hours after Putin held trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.
