articles.headline: Is Raphael Warnock running for president?
keyFacts: Sen. Raphael Warnock stated he is keeping options open regarding a potential 2028 Democratic presidential bid.
Warnock explained that Democrats can win in the South by visiting rural communities and building multiracial coalitions around shared concerns.
Warnock emphasized that resolving tough international issues like the Israeli-Palestinian conflict requires strong American presidential leadership.
body: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA) has kept the door open on a presidential bid. | Finn Gomez/Getty Images

The 2026 midterm elections were less than three weeks ago — and the new Democratic congressional majorities chosen by voters are still more than a month from taking office — but if the 2028 Democratic presidential primary isn’t fully underway, then at the very least, potential candidates are already starting to jockey for position.

Some of that maneuvering was on display earlier this month at the fittingly named “What’s Next” political conference in Denver. The conference drew Democratic operatives, strategists, and presidential hopefuls from around the country — and Vox’s America, Actually podcast, where host Astead Herndon asked attendees for their thoughts about Democratic Party’s future.

Herndon also sat down with one possible 2028 candidate: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA). His background is especially relevant after the midterms: He’s the senior pastor at the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta at a time when more Democratic candidates are embracing religious appeals ; and he’s a student of the civil rights movement, the legacy of which could be seen in surging Black turnout across the South after the Supreme Court rolled back parts of the Voting Rights Act.
Warnock has kept the door open on a presidential bid ; his colleague Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) is also frequently discussed as a potential candidate .

Herndon and Warnock discussed how Democrats can win in the South following election victories by Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom and others; why Warnock made the trip to Michigan to campaign for Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed; and the need for presidential leadership to resolve some of America’s toughest problems at home and abroad.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel .
I feel like some of the reason the South hasn’t seen some of that investment is a presumption that white Southerners are unpersuadable.

And in your race, and I think what happened in Georgia, it wasn’t just turnout, but it was also persuasion. It was convincing people to move on from Republicans and embrace Democrats. How do you make that persuasion happen?

As a pastor, there’s something that I call the ministry of presence. Sometimes you can’t solve people’s problems because they’re complicated or complex. They may take time, or you may not be able to fix it immediately. But there’s something healing about having people show up for you.

And so when I was running in 2021, and then again had to turn around and run in 2022, I would show up in these little towns all across Georgia. The folks were surprised that I was there. And you might be thinking, “Well, of course they were surprised that a Democrat was there.” No, they were surprised that anybody running for the United States Senate was in their little town.

And as we sat down and talked about their hospital that had just closed, as we talked about the struggles that their farmers were having under the tariffs that Trump imposed in his first term, we realized that we had things in common, and we shared a faith. And I got enough of those voters to build the kind of moral, multiracial coalition to win.
Some of the playbook here, though, feels kind of intuitive. You know, show up, lean in to a kind of shared identity. Campaign everywhere.

Even when I’ve heard Southerners talk about building structures over a long period of time, part of me wonders: Why has it been such an effort to make that happen? Are we talking around racism here? Is it just because these are people who have been written off?

That’s a good point, and it’s an interesting thing. Here’s what Black Southerners and white Southerners have in common — particularly poor white Southerners in these rural districts: They’re written off. Like, that’s a shared identity. And if we’re ever to have a moment in this country that transforms it into something that Dr. King called the beloved community, we’ll somehow traverse those boundaries and recognize how much we have in common and how much our interests are connected.

I thought it was really interesting how you went to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, who obviously was victorious in that race. You made a clear pitch to Black voters. I thought it was an interesting message. I want you to just describe it — why was that advocacy important to you?

First of all, I wanted us to win the majority. But also, as I looked at that debate as it was unfolding, I had to show up. I’m a child of the Black church. And when we say the Black church, let me hasten because people don’t know this history.

We’ve never meant anything racially exclusive about that. Black church is just a moniker for the anti-slavery church. Because almost all of American Christianity acquiesced — not just acquiesced, aided and provided a kind of moral covering, if you will, for slavery. So the Black church was literally born fighting for freedom. It was born fighting bigotry.
“We need somebody who doesn’t need the job; who really is driven by a deep sense of moral vocation and mission, and for whom the job is a set of tools.”

And when I saw the all-out assault on Brother Abdul on the basis of his religious identity — bigotry is bigotry, and religious bigotry is bigotry. The Black church was born fighting bigotry. And so you literally have people saying that he’s unfit because of where he prays and how he prays.
And if there was anybody that I felt should be the tip of the spear rejecting that idea, it was the Black church, and so I went, among other things, to remind my colleagues there of who we are.

It wasn’t just Republicans who used some of those Islamophobic attacks. There was the infamous scene of Haley Stevens , the Democratic congresswoman who lost that primary, going to the Black church [with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers].
Here she is standing with somebody who is engaged in this kind of Islamophobic rhetoric, and she’s in a Black church doing this. It’s deeply insulting.

We had Abdul El-Sayed on our show , and he made the case for cutting off aid to Israel. In 2025, you and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff voted to block a measure from Bernie Sanders that would’ve stopped $8 billion in aid for Israel.
I recently saw a stat that 74 percent of Democrats oppose additional funding for Israel, per a poll from the New York Times and Siena . Was that vote a mistake?
We’ve had several [Joint Resolution of Disapproval] votes. You chose only to mention the one that I didn’t vote for. I have voted on multiple occasions to limit military aid to Israel.

My North Star where that issue is concerned is a region where Israeli mothers and Palestinian mothers can put their children to sleep at night, know that they’re safe, and have them awaken to a world that embraces their full humanity.

I support a two-state solution. Clearly, Netanyahu does not. He is a problem. and what we need in this moment is leadership. I don’t shirk that one bit. But I will tell you this, as someone who has voted for these [joint resolutions] on a few occasions in response to the moral atrocities that we’ve seen in Gaza, I can tell you that what I’ve learned is that there is no replacement for presidential leadership, and we haven’t had that on this issue in quite some time.
Would you include President Biden in that?
We have not had the kind of leadership that I would want to see on that issue in quite some time. The people are crying out for more.
I am just old enough to remember when an American president took two old men in a room at Camp David and he wouldn’t let them go until they worked something out.

Of course, Anwar Sadat paid a very high price for that. I remember that, too. I think I was in seventh grade. We need American presidential leadership in this moment for that and for a whole range of reasons.
You’ve mentioned presidential leadership. What’s one nonnegotiable for the next Democratic presidential nominee? What’s one thing you think they have to do?

We need somebody who doesn’t need the job; who really is driven by a deep sense of moral vocation and mission, and for whom the job is a set of tools. But the mission is what is central. I think when you have somebody who’s grounded in that kind of deep commitment, then we’re onto something.

I’ve seen you kind of dodge this question about whether you’re considering a run for president in 2028. Your go-to answer was, “Well, I’m focused on the midterms.” Now that we have results from the midterms, I’m going ask you again.
Are you thinking about running for president in 2028?
I remain very committed, and deeply honored to be in this fight for the people of Georgia.
You know, who gets to represent 11 million people? Stand up, get up, fight for them every day? And I remain prayerful about what’s the best use of my gifts in this moment.
I hope that at the end of my life, I will have poured it all out and gone ’till the wheels fall off. And that’s what I’m trying to do — give it all I have.
Give me a sense of how that decision calculus works. Very few people are ever in the position to think about such a thing. How do you go about making a decision about whether that’s true for you?
I have been praying this prayer since I was a kid. I ask God to order my steps. And so you just do the work, and I think you’ll know what you need to do when the time comes.

articles.headline: Quentin Tarantino's Western Thriller Masterpiece Is Officially Free on Streaming
keyFacts: Quentin Tarantino's 2015 Western thriller The Hateful Eight is currently available to stream for free with ads on Tubi.
The film follows a group of untrustworthy characters stranded by a blizzard in a Wyoming haberdashery, leading to a violent mystery.
The article states that the movie combines the style of Django Unchained with the contained, whodunit narrative of Reservoir Dogs.
body: As far as Quentin Tarantino movies go, just about everyone loves Pulp Fiction. Reservoir Dogs and Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood are also widely regarded, while the Kill Bill films and Django Unchained each have a pretty fervent fanbase. But with so many great entries in his filmography, it’s inevitable that at least a few of his movies would get lost in the shuffle. One of those often overlooked films is his 2015 Western thriller, which may not be top-tier Tarantino, but it’s still an excellent film that combines the strengths of two of his previous entries.
A blizzard turns Tarantino’s Western into a whodunit

The Hateful Eight, which is currently free to stream (with ads) on Tubi, takes place in the 1870s in the wintry Wyoming Territory. Kurt Russell is John "the Hangman" Ruth, a bounty hunter bringing in Daisy Domergue (Jennifer Jason Leigh), a gang member with a big price on her head. He’ll collect his bounty in the town of Red Rock, with a stopover at a place called Minnie's Haberdashery on the way, but Ruth’s driver (James Parks) has to stay ahead of an impending blizzard.

On the way to Minnie’s, Ruth’s carriage picks up two unexpected passengers, both of whom lost their horses in the snow and will surely die in the blizzard. First there’s Major Marquis Warren (Samuel L. Jackson), a fellow bounty hunter and former Union Army general who keeps a personal letter to him from Abraham Lincoln in his breast pocket. The second unexpected passenger is Chris Mannix (Walton Goggins), the new sheriff of Red Rock and the son of a Confederate war hero. While Ruth is suspicious of both of them, he decides to let them join him on the way to Minnie’s.

Once they arrive at Minnie’s, however, Minnie isn’t there. Instead, the haberdashery has apparently been left in the care of a Mexican man named Señor Bob (Demián Bichir) while Minnie is visiting her mother. Also present are three other men that Warren, a frequent guest of Minnie’s, doesn’t recognize. As the entire group is snowed in for the night, it’s eventually revealed that nobody is quite who they say they are and bloodshed ultimately ensues.

Like I said, The Hateful Eight is not top-tier Tarantino. Tarantino’s best work has generally come when he’s charting new territory for himself. Inglourious Basterds was his first war movie, and with its heist-like plot and unabashed joy in rewriting history, it showed what Tarantino could do with that genre. Django Unchained was his first Western, and, with its heavy influence from Spaghetti Westerns and Tarantino’s trademark talkative, over-the-top characters and depiction of extreme violence, it showed what a Tarantino Western looks like.
The Hateful Eight doesn’t do that. In fact, it can pretty easily be summed up in classic Hollywood this-meets-that fashion: The Hateful Eight is Django Unchained meets Reservoir Dogs.
The Hateful Eight is Django Unchained meets Reservoir Dogs

It being another Western with broad, loud, talkative characters, it has the same feel as Django Unchained. Originally, The Hateful Eight was a Django sequel called Django in White Hell, but Tarantino found that Django didn’t fit the story. And while Django isn't in it, it’s clear that this movie is in the same ballpark.

As for the Reservoir Dogs part of it, it is narratively similar, with it being tightly contained primarily in one location, with a bunch of untrustworthy characters who don’t really know each other very well. It’s also a bit of a whodunit, just like Reservoir Dogs is with its “Who’s the rat?” plot thread.

None of this is to say that The Hateful Eight isn't a good movie — not at all. The Hateful Eight is an expertly crafted film which begins with a slow burn and delivers surprise after surprise once the bullets start flying. The movie blends a lot of genres, with elements of a Western, a thriller, and even a bit of broad comedy, but it's most effective as a mystery. Not only does the plot slowly unravel as Ruth tries to figure out who he can trust, but each of the characters does, too.

Speaking of those characters, there are no good guys in the movie, but there are a lot of bad guys you end up rooting for because they are incredibly entertaining to watch. Samuel L. Jackson’s character is joyously funny, and Kurt Russell’s hangman is a mean grouch with a strange but consistent set of principles. Also, Walton Goggins, who was previously in Django, racks up another memorable Tarantino character in this movie. (Let’s hope he shows up in Tarantino’s 10th flick and takes a break from those damn Walmart commercials already).

While it stays firmly within previously charted territory for Tarantino, The Hateful Eight is very entertaining and very funny. It has all the hallmarks of a great Tarantino movie, with lots of fun characters, over-the-top violence, and unexpected plot twists. It may not be top-tier Tarantino, but it’s a really good time.

articles.headline: “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science
keyFacts: US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs during the World Economic Forum meeting in Davos.
Racial views of human nature are re-emerging in Western politics, fuelling far-right propaganda and misinformation strategies on social media.
A network of people produces methodologically flawed work claiming to show innate differences among racial groups and manages to publish it in some mainstream academic journals.
body: At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).

These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.

These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.

What got less attention was that Cofnas has links to a network of people who make supposedly scientific claims about the innate intelligence, criminality, or sexuality of different racial groups. Some within this network are affiliated with universities, giving their work the mask of legitimacy.

This group produces work that has the appearance of science, but which is methodologically deeply flawed and fails to engage with rigorous scientific research. Yet they regularly succeed in publishing this work in (a handful of) mainstream academic journals.
How do they manage to do this, and what are the consequences?

articles.headline: This is how badly Trump’s Republican endorsements did in the midterms
keyFacts: In the 2026 midterms, half of Donald Trump's endorsed Senate candidates and most endorsed governors lost, according to a Guardian analysis.
Democrats flipped more than 45 House seats, nine Senate seats, and six governor's offices amid voter disapproval of Trump's agenda.
Prominent conservatives, including Elon Musk, have begun backing away from Trump's MAGA agenda following the Republican election losses.
body: Donald Trump often boasts about the power of his “Complete and Total Endorsement” of candidates, but in the 2026 midterms, his endorsements carried less weight than they did two years ago.

Half of the Senate candidates Trump endorsed lost, and most of the governors the US president endorsed were defeated by Democratic candidates in this month’s blue wave midterm elections, according to an analysis by the Guardian.
With almost every race now called, Democrats flipped more than 45 House seats, nine Senate seats and six governor’s offices.
The Guardian previously analyzed Trump’s endorsements immediately after the election. In the weeks after the midterms, more races have been called, showing Trump-endorsed candidates underperformed.

The election results reflect voters’ widespread disapproval of Trump, who has steered the US into a conflict with Iran, imposed tariffs on some of the US’s biggest trading allies, pushed the boundaries of his executive authority, overseen an aggressive mass deportation agenda and directed focus to his personal construction projects.
Trump seemingly brushed aside voters’ rebuke of his agenda, claiming Republicans would have won had his name been on the ballot.

Trump’s influence over the Republican party, which he molded in the shape of his Maga party since rising to power in 2016, is dwindling. In 2024, just 35% of Trump-endorsed Senate candidates lost, according to Ballotpedia. But in 2026, 50% of Trump-endorsed Senate candidates lost.

Voters’ rejection of Trump was underlined by the fact that his hand-picked candidates lost in traditionally conservative states. It was especially noticeable because the US president had interjected himself in contentious primaries.

In Texas, Trump roiled Republicans in the state by refusing to endorse the incumbent senator, John Cornyn, and instead backing Ken Paxton, a loyal ally with a controversial past, in the party’s primary. Cornyn, a traditional Republican, was largely considered the safer option.
In South Carolina, Trump hand-picked Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, despite her having no formal political experience.
Historically, Trump’s gubernatorial endorsements perform worse than his Senate or House endorsements. Still, more of his picks lost in 2026 than in the 2022 midterms.
Just nine of the 23 endorsed Republicans won their races, four of whom were incumbents. Every Trump-endorsed gubernatorial candidate lost in races considered a “toss-up” by Cook Political Report.
In 2022, 10 of the 21 endorsed Republicans won their races, according to Ballotpedia.

Approximately 70% of the House candidates Trump endorsed won, though the US president often endorses incumbent candidates running in Republican districts. In 2024, 86% of Trump-endorsed House candidates won their elections, according to data from Ballotpedia.
When analyzing the performance of Trump-endorsed House candidates in competitive districts, most lost to Democratic opponents.
Every single candidate Trump endorsed in districts rated a “toss-up” by Cook Political Report lost.
In the 18 districts rated “lean Republican”, nine Trump-endorsed candidates lost, while eight won.

(As of Thursday, the Associated Press had not called four House races where Trump endorsed a candidate. In one race, Minnesota’s first congressional district, which is rated “lean Republican”, the Democratic candidate was narrowly leading.)
Even in districts that Republicans gerrymandered as part of Trump’s nationwide mid-decade redistricting effort, Democrats managed to hold on to seats.

The reckoning has led some prominent conservatives to back away from Trump’s Maga agenda, including Elon Musk, who once held a top position in the administration and spent nearly $500m on Republican candidates in the midterms.
“I’m not MAGA,” Musk told the New York Times on Wednesday during the DealBook Summit.

Even JD Vance widely believed to be considering a run in 2028, acknowledged that the war with Iran hurt Republicans in the midterms. Though the US vice-president did not directly state he was backing away from Trump, his statement did acknowledge the impact of the president’s policies.

articles.headline: Rail safety legislation within reach for Senate Democrats after midterm blue tsunami
keyFacts: Senate Democrats expect rail safety legislation to pass next Congress after gaining nine seats in the midterm elections.
Sen. Maria Cantwell and a White House official confirmed the Railway Safety Act is a priority for Senate Democrats and President Donald Trump.
The Association of American Railroads will lobby against specific bill language, including two-person crew requirements, citing potential added costs.
body: A Republican wipeout in the midterm elections means that rail safety legislation has a real shot of passing the Senate next Congress, when Democrats will be four votes shy of a supermajority.

Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA) told the Washington Examiner the Railway Safety Act is “absolutely” a priority as she prepares to lead the Senate Commerce Committee again, and she expects leadership will give it a floor vote, either as part of the bipartisan highway bill or some other piece of must-pass legislation.
“I see it moving,” said Cantwell, who took an active role in negotiations when the legislation, crafted in the wake of the East Palestine train disaster, was first introduced in 2023.
With Democrats controlling 56 Senate seats next year, it might even survive a stand-alone vote on the Senate floor, although that whip count is fluid.

Sens. Eric Schmitt (R-MO) and Josh Hawley (R-MO), two early GOP co-sponsors, said they still support the bill. The next most likely GOP backer is Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH). He hails from Ohio, the site of the train derailment, and co-sponsored the latest iteration of the legislation.
Moreno was noncommittal on that support, however, in a brief Tuesday interview, saying twice that “I’ll have to take a look at that.”

One industry insider speculated that Moreno may be reluctant to partner with Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown, the Ohio Democrat he unseated in 2024, now that he’s leading Senate Republicans’ campaign arm. Brown, who is returning to the Senate after a successful comeback bid, will be up for election again in two years.

The last time the Railway Safety Act came close to the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster, Vice President JD Vance and Brown were in the Senate and two Republicans short of reaching that threshold.

All 51 Democrats supported the legislation, as did seven GOP senators — a feat given it’s the sort of union-friendly bill that Republicans traditionally oppose. The legislation sets crew requirements and imposes new civil penalties for rail safety violations, among other provisions.
SENATE TAPS BRAKES ON RAIL SAFETY BILL AHEAD OF SHERROD BROWN ELECTION

Many of those Republicans, Vance included, no longer serve in the Senate, and the bill never went anywhere after passing out of the Commerce Committee in 2023. It was shelved completely under Chairman Ted Cruz (R-TX) after the 2024 election, when Republicans retook control of the chamber.

But Democrats will have an easier time after capturing nine Senate seats in the midterm elections, a shock outcome that puts Republicans firmly in the minority for the next two years, and probably longer .

“I would just say Republicans are going to be in a tough position,” Hawley told the Washington Examiner . “They’re not going to be in a position to extract a lot of concessions on a lot of these things.”

In the House, Democrats picked up more than 40 seats and will also have a commanding majority. The expected chairman of the House Transportation Committee, Rep. Rick Larsen (D-WA), has named the Railway Safety Act as a priority in the new Congress, a break from the current GOP chairman, Rep. Sam Graves (R-MO).
Their panel can also expect a new round of lobbying from President Donald Trump, who successfully pushed for its adoption as part of a highway bill markup earlier this year.
The legislation never reached the House floor, but it stands a better chance of passing with Democrats in charge of Congress and Trump in office.
A White House official confirmed that Trump “supports the enactment of the Railway Safety Act Amendment next Congress.”
“This is a priority for this administration,” said the official.
On the other side of the fight is the rail industry, which has said it is not opposed to the legislation in principle, but wants certain language removed, including its two-person crew requirement.
“We have a strong case to make, and we won’t tailor the message only to Republicans,” said Ted Greener, the senior vice president of communications at the Association of American Railroads.

He noted that Senate Democrats’ path to a 56-seat majority runs through agriculture-heavy states such as Kansas and Iowa, and that his group will be pressing them to consider what he said is $30 billion in additional costs for the transportation sector over the span of five years.
Among Republicans, Sen. Jim Banks (R-IN) is another Trump-aligned senator who is undecided on the Railway Safety Act but could be won over.
FETTERMAN TO GET RARE FILIBUSTER BACKUP WITH NEW CROP OF SENATE DEMOCRATS
“I had some questions about it,” Banks said of earlier iterations of the legislation. “If it’s exactly like the Vance bill, I’ll have an open mind about it, but we’ll see.”

The legislation has also traditionally received support from Pennsylvania’s two senators, given that the East Palestine disaster affected communities on the other side of the border with Ohio. Sen. Dave McCormick (R-PA) declined to comment on the bill earlier this week.

articles.headline: Harbinger is building the unsexy EVs that keep the economy moving
keyFacts: Electric truck startup Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D funding round earlier this month.
The company secured a $300 million order from FedEx and a new defense contract with the US military.
Harbinger focuses on building commercial Class 4 to 6 delivery vans and box trucks instead of consumer electric vehicles.
body: While legacy automakers tap the brakes on electric vehicles, one startup is hitting the accelerator. Earlier this month, electric truck maker Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D round, capping a banner stretch that includes a $300 million order from FedEx and a new defense contract with the US military.
Harbinger is building the unsexy EVs that keep the economy moving
Cybertruck who?
Cybertruck who?

Harbinger is stacking up wins by skipping the consumer EV hype cycle altogether and focusing on the unglamorous workhorses that keep the economy running: Class 4–6 delivery vans and box trucks. The company’s thesis is simple: go after the overlooked commercial segments where legacy trucks are weak and giant automakers can’t be bothered to compete, CEO John Harris tells me.

“We’re not solving the big obvious problem because everyone’s going to solve that problem, and as a result, the margins get kind of ground down to zero,” Harris says. “We’re solving problems that — they’ve just been there forever and you no longer think of this as a problem, you just think of it as like part of existence. It’s like a tax on your life.”

Founded in 2021 by veterans of Canoo, QuantumScape, and Faraday Future, Harbinger aims to fill a structural gap in the auto market, in which most passenger EV platforms lack the durability to scale up while the heavy-duty platforms are too heavy and expensive to scale down.
“In auto, you have Class 1 companies and you have Class 8 companies,” Harris says. “And everything in between is kind of a wasteland... It is much, much, much too small for a big company to serve.”

Which is not to say the industry hasn’t tried. Ford and GM both took shots at electrifying the medium-duty segment with the E-Transit and BrightDrop delivery vans, respectively, but sluggish sales and the loss of federal incentives forced them to discontinue or cancel those models.

Harris says that big automakers are ill-suited to task, with their over-reliance on third-party suppliers to build all the necessary components. The effort becomes too spread out and expensive, with not enough return on your investment. That’s why Harbinger is attempting a more vertically integrated approach, he says, assembling its own battery packs and drive units in house — with inverters to follow.

“If you are not vertically integrated in auto, you don’t build viable products,” Harris says. “We believe that electric vehicles are only viable when they’re competitive on acquisition price with combustion vehicles.”

Of course, Harris and his fellow cofounders have tasted failure in their previous ventures. Harbinger’s CTO Phillip Weicker cofounded EV startup Canoo, which ran out of cash and filed bankruptcy in 2025. Harris himself spent a year at tumultuous Chinese EV company Faraday Future before moving on to Xos Trucks and then Palmer Luckey’s Anduril.

“I was an engineer at Faraday. I wasn’t in charge of anything,” Harris says. “So it’s not like, ‘John, why did Faraday not succeed?’ I can tell you lots of reasons, but it wasn’t because the plastic part that I designed didn’t work. It was because the plastic part that I designed was going into a vehicle for which the world customer base was like three people.”

Those companies “fundamentally didn’t work,” he adds, “because of the market fit issue and the leadership issue. Not because the engineering didn’t work or electrification wasn’t ready or they didn’t have enough capital.”

Harbinger’s approach is more pragmatic, offering both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid powertrains for its medium-duty trucks. The company is not pursuing heavy-duty Class 8 trucks like the Tesla Semi, however, as Harris argues the economics of electric long-haul trucking are unworkable.

“Class 8 electrification to me is one of those markets. I completely reject the notion that that’s a good fit for electrification for the majority of the market,” he says. “We can put [the Tesla Semi] on the watch list with the Cybertruck.”

With companies like Amazon and FedEx making serious moves to secure more electric delivery vehicles, Harbinger is well-positioned to be a key supplier. And with diesel prices skyrocketing as a result of the war with Iran, more companies are waking up to a reality in which EVs can help bring down their costs.

Harbinger isn’t just building delivery trucks — it’s also branching into energy storage and military technology. For example, the company supplies battery power systems to Airstream and partners with American Rheinmetall and Forterra to build self-driving hybrid supply vehicles for the US Army. Harbinger also recently bought Phantom AI to bring advanced driver-assistance features to commercial fleets, in the hopes of giving companies a clear, measurable return on their safety investments.

With millions in fresh capital and major contracts already on the books, Harbinger has cleared the first major hurdle that tripped up its founders’ past ventures. Now comes the hardest part in the auto business: proving it can actually build them at scale.

“Auto is a big enough opportunity that it can get people’s attention,” Harris says. “It’s also punishingly difficult. So if you can make something that works in auto, it will be phenomenal in every other segment, because every other segment, the competition is essentially weaker.”

articles.headline: Dem Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear under fire from state auditor over waste, fraud, abuse fears
keyFacts: Kentucky State Auditor Ball accused Gov. Andy Beshear of failing to address $1.5 billion in taxpayer waste identified by her office.
Gov. Andy Beshear's office rejected Ball's claims as inaccurate, citing six consecutive budget surpluses and fiscal upgrades under his administration.
Auditor Ball said she sees a tremendous opportunity heading into 2027 to stop state waste and fraud as public concern rises.
body: Dem Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear under fire from state auditor over waste, fraud, abuse fears
By
Andrew Mark Miller, Fox News
Published Nov. 21, 2026, 6:54 a.m. ET
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Kentucky’s top auditor says her office has uncovered $1.5 billion in taxpayer waste across state government and accused Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, widely believed to have presidential aspirations, of brushing off the findings instead of helping fix them.

“I wish I could say that I had more support and help from the governor’s office in Kentucky, but I haven’t really and that’s one of the reasons why I’m very public with our reports,” Ball said in an interview this week at a State Financial Officers Foundation (SFOF) conference in Philadelphia.
“I’m very public with our findings, because I need the public’s help.”
Advertisement

“I need the backlash that comes when you see money just being flushed down the toilet, when you see that you’re losing money, especially in Medicaid. It’s money that should go to people who are actually in need, and we’re losing those dollars.”

Over the past year, Ball’s office flagged $836 million in wasteful Medicaid spending that was primarily driven by multi-state concurrent enrollment, where Kentucky continued paying monthly managed care capitation fees for individuals simultaneously enrolled in Medicaid in up to eight other states.

Her audits also flagged ineligible noncitizens receiving benefits, single Social Security numbers being used by up to 10 people at once, duplicate individual payments, and roughly $100 million in SNAP benefit errors, bringing the total waste she cited across state benefit programs to $1.5 billion.
Advertisement

“I have had conversations with the governor’s staff,” Ball explained. “We are always letting the governor know, ‘Hey, this is what we found.’ We also offer solutions all the time. And typically what I get back is, like for the $836 million of Medicaid dollars that we found, is that, ‘Well, that happens everywhere. You know, that’s not unique to us.’

“And that’s really a troubling response. If your attitude is like, ‘Well, it’s not just us, you know, we’re not really doing a horrible job because it happens other places too,’ that explains why problems like this continue.”

Additionally, Ball’s office released a report earlier this year outlining spending by Beshear’s executive branch in fiscal year 2025 that, while not illegal, flagged what she called “massive” issues of extravagant spending of tax dollars that “needs to stop.”
Advertisement

The “concerning expenditures” listed include $183,576 in out-of-state travel costs, including $7,632 for a limousine in Germany; a $17,013 dinner at a Kentucky distillery; and $360,000 for 75 people to attend a two-day conference within the Commonwealth.

“I think one thing that I have realized is that the governor doesn’t like bad news. And unfortunately, a lot of times when I come in, and I do an audit, the news that I have is bad,” Ball said. “But what I also try to remind people, it’s good too, in the sense that I also have a recommendation for how to fix it.

“So, while it is important to identify the problems — and I do that — I’m also hyper-focused on the solution. And I would encourage the governor to jump in and help me be part of the solution to this. That’s not been the experience that I’ve had. I’ve not had cooperation, and I would love to have that. I think that that’s what Kentuckians deserve.”
Advertisement

Beshear’s office has repeatedly pushed back on Ball’s criticisms, dismissing her $836 million Medicaid waste estimate as “a wild extrapolation from a small subset” and maintaining that once Kentucky gained access to updated federal cross-check databases, actual multi-state overlap numbers were “nothing remotely close to that.”

In a statement to Fox News Digital, his office said the governor has “created a fiscally responsible administration, securing six consecutive budget surpluses, the five best years on record for economic investment and upgrades from all three major bond rating agencies while also cutting income and property taxes.
“His management of the state is delivering positive results, so hardworking Kentuckians can live better lives.”
Advertisement

Beshear’s office added that Ball’s report has “significant errors and inaccuracies” and suggested she focus on “real threats looming in Kentucky due to Trump’s ‘Big, Ugly Bill,’ which risks the closure of 35 rural hospitals, the jobs of 20,000 healthcare workers and health coverage for thousands of Kentuckians.”
When it comes to potential Medicaid waste, fraud and abuse, Ball told Fox News Digital it is unlikely that money can be clawed back, heightening the importance of stopping it before it begins.

The Trump administration has made cracking down on fraud this year and set up the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud in March which has reported that federal agencies have identified $260.7 billion in estimated fraud since January 2025.
Advertisement

Ball told Fox News Digital that heading into 2027, she sees a “tremendous opportunity” to address waste, fraud, and abuse in Kentucky because the “public cares right now, I think, at a level that they’ve not cared before.”

“I’ve always cared about protecting taxpayer dollars, I’ve also cared about stopping waste, fraud, and abuse. I care about complying with the law,” Ball said. “I think this is this beautiful moment right now where the public deeply cares about it too.

“So I think I have an opportunity. I think other auditors around the country, other people who are in similar roles, have opportunities like it’s never been before where we really can take the effort to stop these things from happening.”

articles.headline: Expedition 33 lead writer says Grand Theft Auto 6 layoff concerns show that 'people creating the value do not receive a proportionate amount of that value'
keyFacts: Rockstar developers working on Grand Theft Auto 6 are concerned about potential layoffs despite the game's massive commercial success.
Jennifer Svedberg-Yen stated that financial profits from games do not fairly reach the creative teams who generate the value.
Rockstar employees are currently voting on whether to unionize in an effort to address job security and compensation issues.
body: Grand Theft Auto 6 is already enormously successful, having enjoyed "the biggest entertainment launch in history". But the current games industry is such that some Rockstar developers are still concerned about being laid off in the wake of its release. Writing for the Guardian prior to GTA 6's launch, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte explained that although there is "no indication that layoffs are coming" it nonetheless "says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off."

It might sound odd for the developers of such a hugely successful game to be worried about losing their jobs, but layoffs don't just occur when games or companies struggle commercially. A common cause of layoffs in the games industry is companies trying to reduce overheads after a game has launched, as the studio switches from full production to post-release support for their current game and planning for the next one.

It's partly why the industry seems to be in a constant, rolling state of layoffs, even when games appear to sell well. This issue was recently addressed by Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, the lead writer of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Svedberg-Yen, who left Sandfall Interactive in July, claimed that the problem is exacerbated by an imbalance in who benefits financially when a game like Grand Theft Auto 6 launches.

"99 Metacritic score. Multiple award nominations before it even released. Massive sales and player engagement. Incredible amounts of tangible and intangible value creation. Yet the team is worried about layoffs," Svedberg-Yen wrote in an Instagram post. "So, who receives the lion's share of the profits from their labor? Not the vast majority of the creative team."

Svedberg-Yen pointed out that this is "one of the issues that happens when the people creating the value do not receive a proportionate amount of that value," adding that "In finance, we call that value extraction."

Svedberg-Yen also commented on the Rockstar team's ongoing efforts to unionise, with the team in the process of voting on whether or not it wants a union. If successful, the Rockstar Game Workers Union would become the biggest in the UK's gaming sector.

"I sincerely hope the Rockstar team is successful in unionizing," Svedberg-Yen wrote. "Layoffs during lulls in development cycles would work a lot better if teams were properly paid for the value they create, not just one-time, but throughout the life of the thing they created."
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The games industry has seen a huge number of layoffs in the last few years. A recent report by GDC found that 34% of developers it surveyed had been laid off since 2024. Xbox alone has cut thousands of jobs, with more planned going into January 2027. Most recently, Firaxis, owned by GTA 6 publisher Take Two Interactive, reportedly laid off a third of its staff earlier this week as it works on a new XCOM.

Rick has been fascinated by PC gaming since he was seven years old, when he used to sneak into his dad's home office for covert sessions of Doom. He grew up on a diet of similarly unsuitable games, with favourites including Quake, Thief, Half-Life and Deus Ex. Between 2013 and 2022, Rick was games editor of Custom PC magazine and associated website bit-tech.net. But he's always kept one foot in freelance games journalism, writing for publications like Edge, Eurogamer, the Guardian and, naturally, PC Gamer. While he'll play anything that can be controlled with a keyboard and mouse, he has a particular passion for first-person shooters and immersive sims.
