articles.headline: ChatGPT shrunk down to run on a Super Nintendo
keyFacts: Tech journalist Benj Edwards created a tiny version of ChatGPT that runs on a Super Nintendo cartridge.
Edwards stated that the experimental model is not a useful assistant because it is tiny, knows about 8,000 words, and frequently makes mistakes.
Edwards plans to pursue new ideas to make tiny models even more coherent.
body: If you’ve ever wondered how small an instance of ChatGPT could get, wonder no longer. Someone has actually rigged up a tiny version of the chatbot to run on a Super Nintendo cartridge.

Tech journalist and retro tech enthusiast Benj Edwards is responsible for ChatGPT for SNES . He's published it online running in an emulator, complete with SNES-era music and sound effects, and for download as an SNES ROM, too.

It’s not a big model, mind you, and performance is thus pretty limited: According to the website, it’s a 2.2 million-parameter offshoot of OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-120b, which was used to develop its training conversations – so in that sense it truly is a ChatGPT that runs on an SNES cartridge. Edwards described it to The Register as a distilled version of the aforementioned open-weight model.

There are two options built into ChatGPT for SNES: One that’s purely the model, with every word generated coming right from its tiny little silicon brain, and another that includes a fact book culled from the opening sentences of around 150,000 simple English Wikipedia articles. If you opt to run both versions and ask it the same questions, you’ll notice a massive difference.

Given some of the other responses we got while testing, there’s really no good reason to run the base model – memory isn’t really an issue given the basic build is about 4MB and the factbook build is just 19MB.
Edwards admits that it’s not the most helpful AI model, either – this is just an experiment after all.

“It is not a useful assistant: the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT, knows about 8,000 words, and often gets things wrong, sometimes confidently,” Edwards noted in his writeup. In that sense, it really is vintage AI on vintage hardware. “The fact book can carry mistakes too.”

If you have an SNES lying around (lucky you), you can download the ROM from this link. If you want to get it running on an SNES you’ll need a cartridge that allows running of custom ROMs, and that supports Nintendo’s Super FX graphics coprocessor. Cartridges like the FXPak Pro and SD2SNES support it. The factbook version also requires support for the aftermarket Media Streaming Unit 1 (MSU-1), which adds CD-ROM like features to the SNES. MSU-1 is available in both of the flash carts mentioned above.
If you have some real hardware skills, however, you could technically make your own ChatGPT cartridge.

“The ‘pure’ version, which generates all responses from the AI language model, could run from a real custom SNES cart,” Edwards told us – it doesn’t even actually need the Super FX chip. “I do have a version of ChatGPT for SNES that can run without the Super FX chip, but without the extra processing power the answers are not as good.”
That said, Edwards believes its absolutely crazy and nonsensical answers are part of the fun.
“ChatGPT for SNES can definitely make mistakes too, but it's almost cute when it does it because of its limited knowledge and its playful interface,” Edwards told us.

While a human may have designed the experiment, the coding work was done by AI, Edwards told us – he’s been interested in it since the 1990s and is pursuing more experiments with tiny AI models using the help of the bigger ones.

“I've been theorizing about what I call ‘tiny talking machines’ … over the past year,” Edwards told us, and he’s been able to use coding agents to turn those ideas into actual software. ChatGPT for SNES is one example, and he also created an NES ROM called Séance that uses an even smaller AI model able to run on an original Nintendo Entertainment System that simulates talking to a ghost in a haunted game cartridge.

“I designed the scope of what the software should be, how it should work broadly, what chip it should use, how the interface should look and work, and the sounds it makes when it types responses,” Edwards told us. He added that he sees the project as an AI/human collaboration, which is where he believes AI works best.

“The AI agents who did the coding for this project currently advise that we've hit the limit of how good the AI model can be on the limited hardware,” Edwards said - he’s not taking their word for it, though. “It's up to human creativity to transcend those assumptions. I have already come up with new ideas that I believe can make a tiny model like ChatGPT for SNES even more coherent, and I'm working on them now.” ®

articles.headline: Millions could lose paid benefits due to Congress ignoring decades of Social Security warnings: experts
keyFacts: In 1977, Congress tied Social Security benefit growth to wages despite expert warnings of a future solvency crisis.
Experts warn Social Security's trust fund could run dry by 2032, threatening benefit cuts for millions of Americans.
Experts say Congress will be forced to address the funding shortfall before 2032, possibly by raising taxes.
body: A panel filled with top economists, including a Nobel Peace Prize winner, warned Congress decades ago that their reforms to Social Security could spell disaster.
Now, experts tell Fox News Digital that group from a bygone era was right, as the safety-net program hurtles toward a crisis that could affect millions.

"Social Security benefits were put on autopilot back in 1977," Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow of the American Enterprise Institute, told Fox News Digital. "Since then, Congress has done as little as it possibly could."

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., unveiled a report on the decades-old program that blasted it as a "Ponzi scheme," and warned that Social Security’s slide into insolvency began in the 1970s, when, despite warnings, lawmakers opted to tie benefit growth to wages rather than inflation.
AMERICANS MISLED ON SOCIAL SECURITY FOR DECADES AS CLOCK COUNTS DOWN ON BENEFITS, EXPLOSIVE REPORT REVEALS
Johnson wrote in his report that at the time, an expert panel was formed that warned lawmakers that if they were to tie benefits to inflation, "Social Security would likely be sustainable today."
Still, lawmakers at the time ran with their own amendments to the program, which were signed into law by former President Jimmy Carter in December 1977.

"What they said in 1977 was if you index benefit growth to wages, you're effectively building a solvency crisis into the program," Biggs said. "You are over-promising, you're going to build in benefits that the current system can't afford to pay, and you're committing future taxpayers to pay rates of taxes that the taxpayers in 1977 weren't willing to pay."
In the decades since, Congress has done little to change the program.
SENATE REPUBLICANS BREAK THROUGH WASHINGTON GRIDLOCK WITH MASSIVE AMERICAN ENERGY, DATA CENTER OVERHAUL
Romina Boccia, the Cato Institute’s director of budget and entitlement policy, told Fox News Digital that’s largely because lawmakers have not had the political will to do it.

She agreed with Johnson that Social Security was effectively a "Ponzi scheme," and said "there's this misconception that a lot of Americans think that Social Security is a retirement savings program."

"But for that, you would actually need to have savings occur in the system, and there would need to be assets that would be invested in earning returns," Boccia said. "That's not the case. We're talking about a pay-as-you-go program."
One of the side effects of Congress’ lack of action to rein in the program is that the wage growth formula relies on workers in the economy contributing with their paychecks.
Boccia noted that as the decades have gone on, "We've seen a severe decline in the number of workers compared to the number of retirees collecting benefits as a result of a decline in fertility."
DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN
Congress’ last real successful effort to reform Social Security came in the early 1980s, Biggs noted, when lawmakers were forced to step in to deal with the "funding crisis" hitting the program.
"They raised taxes. They increased the retirement age. So they did this with months to spare to fix Social Security," Biggs said. "It's not something they wanted to do, but they were forced to do."

"Now in 2032, we're going to face the same situation, where Congress will be forced to take action sometime before the trust fund runs out in 2032, not because they want to, but because they're forced to do it," he continued.
If Social Security’s trust fund runs dry by 2032, Americans’ benefits would be slashed and the onus of paying for the shortfall would add trillions more to the nation’s debt.

But Johnson, in his report, declared that the Social Security problem could not be fixed between now and then because of Congress’ inaction for the last several decades, and he suggested that the solution would be to repeal a possible benefits reduction as the program’s trust fund heads toward insolvency in just under seven years.

Biggs, who was part of former President George W. Bush’s effort to reform Social Security over two decades ago, said that had Congress taken action "25 years ago, you could fix Social Security in barely noticeable ways."

"There is no easy fix to Social Security today, and that stems entirely from the fact that every year, when Congress has had the opportunity to fix Social Security, they chose to duck the issue for political reasons and kick the can down the road," Biggs said.
Boccia disagreed with Johnson’s solution and contended that the real answer was one that lawmakers of yesterday and today would be hesitant to approach — raising taxes.

"The real way to think about this is that there's almost no way to imagine Congress would let those benefit cuts take effect," Boccia said. "It will be so politically toxic. So most likely they're going to try to find a different solution."

"The last time the trust fund was running out of money in 1982, Congress put together a commission and then voted on a bill that increased taxes and reduced benefits, including raising the social security retirement age," she continued. "The problem is that the funding gap now is much larger, more than two times bigger than it was in the ‘80s."

articles.headline: Trump insists he's "not rushing to make any decisions on Iran"
keyFacts: Sources told CBS News that the U.S. and Israel are considering a short-term military offensive against Iran.
Two tankers were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, according to the British maritime agency UKMTO.
The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted three Houthi ballistic missiles targeted at Riyadh on Saturday.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:
- President Trump told an Israeli TV network on Thursday that he is "not rushing" and could wait until 2027 to make a decision on his next move in the .

- Despite Mr. Trump's remark, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News Israel and the U.S. are considering in the short term, with the Netanyahu administration concerned about how rapidly Iran is rebuilding its weapons production capacity.

- Iran on Thursday rejected Mr. that it may be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons, with the foreign ministry saying U.S. allegations "keep changing" and are following "the same fraudulent script" as the justification for the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq.
2 tankers attacked in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. maritime agency says
Two tankers were attacked on Saturday in the Strait of Hormuz, at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the United States, British maritime agency UKMTO said.

"A tanker transiting outbound in the Strait of Hormuz has been hit on the stern by an unknown projectile. There are no reported casualties at this time," the agency said, adding that another tanker was struck in its engine room.
Also on Saturday, Iran said it shot down a U.S. drone over Qeshm Island in the strait, according to Iranian state TV.
American fighter jets struck an Iranian missile site on Qeshm last Tuesday, according to a U.S. military official.
Before the Middle East war, triggered by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, one fifth of the world's oil and natural gas passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has since locked down the strait and regularly targets ships that attempt to pass without its authorisation.
Washington, in response, has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, and its navy has been escorting tankers through the waterway.
Saudi-led coalition says it downed 3 Houthi missiles headed for Riyadh

Saudi-led coalition said it downed three Houthi missiles headed for Riyadh after two explosions were heard in the area early on Saturday morning local time, an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital reported.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed (3) ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition said on X.
The blasts came after authorities issued an alert saying the city was "under a hostile aerial threat."
The Saudi civil defense later lifted the alert and declared that "the danger has passed."
Yemen's Houthis said on X that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including in Riyadh.
The incident came after the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis attacked the Red Sea port city of Hodeida and other targets in a "special operation" on Friday.
The Houthis had threatened reprisals.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighboring Yemen's civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
Opposition leader vows to form new Israeli government to oust Netanyahu swiftly
Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next Israeli government, vowed Friday not to let coalition-building talks drag on as his wide-ranging bloc faces divisions on the way forward.

The former military chief's remarks appear as a warning to his own camp, which is split over whether to forge alliances with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, Arab-majority lists, or to form a national unity government that would leave current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the role as a caretaker.
Sources told CBS News this week that a new offensive against Iran in collaboration with the U.S.

"I have no intention of letting this drag on. When the time is right, I will bring a new government before the Knesset for its approval, a good government that I will lead," Eisenkot said in a social media post.

Eisenkot has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu, after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either of them. While denying any attempt to force through a coalition, Eisenkot stressed the need to act fast.

"We are in very dangerous territory. The outgoing prime minister is acting in ways we have never seen before," he said. "Military priorities have become entangled with political interests, and the timetable for military operations with the political calendar."
The AFP contributed reporting.
Tanker in the Strait of Hormuz struck by projectile, says naval monitor
A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by a projectile Friday, causing a fire onboard the vessel but no injuries, according to a British naval monitor.
The tanker was traveling out of the key waterway when it was struck by an unknown projectile, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center.
The UKMTO earlier reported that a bulk carrier traveling east in the Gulf of Aden, off the southern coast of Yemen, had reported shots being fired in its vicinity by assailants on a small boat.
Trump says he, Putin and Xi talked about Iranian nuclear threat
During Friday's news conference, President Trump said that during his trilateral with Russia's President Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping, the three leaders discussed nuclear responsibilities.

Mr. Trump said they "spoke about the need to cooperate to stop the proliferation of that nuclear threat throughout our planet" and that "in particular, we talked extensively about ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."
Trump says U.S. wants "real deal" with Iran
As he lauded slightly lower gas prices at the White House on Friday, President Trump said the U.S. wants a "real deal" with Iran, not a "fake" deal.
"They want to make a deal but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me," he said.
"They've been bulls******g people for 51 years," the president said of Iran.
CENTCOM denies U.S. strike as Iranian news agency reports missile hitting Qeshm Island

U.S. Central Command denied carrying out any new strikes on Iran's strategic Qeshm Island on Friday after Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is closely linked with the country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said a missile had hit the island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Tasnim said it had no information of any possible damage, and other Iranian media outlets offered more vague details. The semi-official Fars news agency said an explosion was heard in the skies over the island, but that the cause was unknown.
The U.S. has attacked the island several times, with what a military official described to CBS News as precision strikes on an IRGC missile site.
The official said that strike was launched "in self-defense … in response to IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets."
Saudi Arabia intercepts 2 Houthi missiles, coalition says
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said Friday that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia backs Yemen's government in the impoverished nation's more than decade-long civil war against the Iran-backed rebel group.

The latest missiles launched by the Houthis targeted the Jazan region, on the southwest Saudi coast near the border with Yemen, but "air defense intercepted and destroyed" them, according to coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki.
The Houthis struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district earlier this week.
Cargo ship reports being fired on by assailants in small boat in Gulf of Aden
A bulk carrier traveling east in the Gulf of Aden, off the southern coast of Yemen, has reported shots being fired in its vicinity by armed men on a small boat, according to a British naval monitor.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center, which is run by the British navy, said Friday that the ship was traveling eastbound when it was approached "by a dark blue skiff with six unidentified, armed persons on board."

"Four shots were fired in quick succession from the skiff and warning shots were returned by the armed security team onboard the bulk carrier," UKTMO said, adding that there was no damage reported to the vessel or its crew.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis issue evacuation warning for Riyadh's financial district
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis urged people to avoid Riyadh's financial district Friday as the group issued a series of threats against Saudi Arabia.

"We announce that (King Abdullah Financial District) in the Saudi enemy's capital, Riyadh, is a military target for our forces. We therefore call on all employees, workers and citizens to stay away from it immediately," military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X.

In a Telegram post Friday, Saree wrote: "We renew our warning to all investment companies, investors and capital to leave Saudi Arabia immediately and move to safe countries. Saudi Arabia is not safe except for the holy areas in Mecca and Medina."
Saudi Arabia of damaging a skyscraper in Riyadh's financial district with a strike earlier this week.
CBS/AFP
U.S. and Israel considering new assault on Iran, sources say
Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new in the short term, according to sources familiar with the matter.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration is concerned about how rapidly the Iranians are rebuilding their ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities and the pace at which Iran is working to shield its military and nuclear infrastructure from attack by moving it underground, the sources told CBS News.

Months of indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have failed to bring a ceasefire deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has refused to even discuss its nuclear program unless the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and accepts six other key conditions.
Israel's military is prepared for a new round of fighting with Iran and is in peak defensive posture to respond to any first attack by Iran, the sources told CBS News.

The Netanyahu administration would prefer to launch a new joint operation with the U.S., but the sources told CBS News it remains unclear whether Mr. Trump wants to order new military action, and if so, what kind.

For both Mr. Trump and Netanyahu, who jointly launched the war with Iran almost nine months ago with a massive round of strikes on the Islamic Republic, the window for any new collaborative action may be closing.
Saudi's fight with Iran-backed Houthis intensifies as civilians warned to evacuate area around Yemeni port

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting in the escalating conflict with Iran's Houthi allies warned civilians Friday to leave the area around the key port of Hodeidah on Yemen's Red Sea coast, which has been held by the rebels for years.

The warning, issued in a social media post by the coalition's Saudi spokesman, suggested Saudi airstrikes on the port could be imminent. It came after Houthi authorities accused Saudi forces of killing 19 people earlier Friday with an attack that hit a civilian boat.

Yemen's civil war flared back up in July as the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran sent regional tension soaring. While the Yemen war started more than a decade ago with the Iran-backed Houthis seizing a huge portion of the country, including capital city Sanaa, it had been relatively calm for years until this summer.

Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi on Friday accused Saudi forces of a "horrific massacre" for the strike on the boat, which the rebels say killed civilians who had been displaced from their homes by the war.

Earlier Friday, the Saudi coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile and two drones fired at the kingdom's southern region, and the Saudi civil defense agency issued warnings of "potential danger" for the cities of Jizan and Abha, as well as the Khamis Mushait Governorate — all in the south.
They later said the danger had passed.
CBS/AFP
Trump's comments on chemical and biological weapons follow "same fraudulent script," Iranian official says

Iran's foreign ministry rejected on Thursday President Trump's accusation that the country may be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons, comparing the claims to then-Secretary of State Colin Powell asserting to the United Nations that Iraq had obtained weapons of mass destruction.

"After the grand narrative of the 'Iranian nuclear threat,' U.S. officials are now claiming that there are indications Iran is developing biological or chemical weapons!" Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X. "The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar. Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."

Baqaei cited the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003, which Washington justified with the claim of weapons of mass destruction being developed by Saddam Hussein's government, and asked why Americans would fall for it again.

"Do American officials really expect the world to forget Colin Powell's infamous appearance before the U.N. Security Council in 2003, when he held up a small vial as a visual representation of the alleged threat posed by Iraq's weapons of mass destruction?" he asked. "That moment has since become an enduring symbol of one of the most consequential intelligence failures and political deceptions in modern history."
"Now we find ourselves facing ominous new allegations and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script," he said.

Mr. Trump on Wednesday said there was an "indication" Iran was looking to develop chemical or biological weapons because the U.S. had "shut them out" of obtaining nuclear weapons, though he offered no evidence to support the claim.
Iran war powers measure again falls short in Senate

The Senate rejected a House-adopted resolution aimed at reining in President Trump's ability to strike Iran, losing Republican support despite frustration with the war following the party's losses in the midterm elections.

In a 48 to 51 vote, three Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky — joined all but one Senate Democrat — Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania — in support of the measure.

Thursday's vote marked the first time either chamber has weighed in on the war since the midterm elections, which dealt Republicans sweeping losses. Voters cited the war in Iran, and its toll on the economy, as among their top concerns.
The resolution would have directed the president "to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran," but its impact would have been largely symbolic.
Trump says he's "not rushing" to make decision on Iran, will wait until new year
President Trump told Channel 12 News in Israel that he is in no hurry to make any decisions on the war with Iran, and could in fact wait until next year.
"I'm not rushing to make any decisions on Iran," Mr. Trump told Keshet 12's Barak Ravid, who spoke to the president as he returned from China. "We'll see what happens after the new year starts."
The story noted Mr. Trump could also change his mind, though.

The tone seems in line with his and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's comments from last week. Mr. Trump called new strikes "quite unlikely," while Rubio said new strikes weren't needed since the economic sanctions campaign was working so well.
In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said he had no need to ask China or Russia for help with an Iran deal.

"They want to make a deal, so I don't need help," Mr. Trump told the network. "I mean, I'm not going to go in asking for help. And frankly, they've treated us very well. They haven't fired. They haven't put ships in the water."

articles.headline: If Trump is Krasnov, Moscow should ask for a refund
keyFacts: Former Georgian security official Emzari Gelashvili analyzed claims that Donald Trump was recruited by the KGB under the code name Krasnov.
Gelashvili argued Trump's tough foreign policy actions against Russian interests contradict allegations that Trump served as a Russian asset.
During a summit in Shenzhen, Chinese officials granted higher diplomatic protocol status to Trump than to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
body: The photographs from Shenzhen had barely gone out before the word came back. Krasnov. The dictator -lover. The man who cannot say no to a strongman. A new Yalta.

I spent 12 years in Georgia’s security services, much of it working against Russian intelligence . In that trade, nobody is convicted by adjectives. You open the file and read what the service received.
So let’s open the file.

“Krasnov” was born on Facebook on Feb. 20, 2025. Alnur Mussayev, a former head of Kazakhstan’s security service, wrote that the KGB had recruited a 40-year-old American businessman named Donald Trump in 1987 under that code name. He offered no document. His own published biographies place him in the Soviet Interior Ministry that year, and the KGB directorate he named handled economic counterintelligence, not foreign recruitment. Even the age is off: Trump was 41 when he first set foot in the Soviet Union that summer.
Robert Mueller had more than 2,800 subpoenas, nearly 500 search warrants, and some 500 witnesses. He did not establish a conspiracy. Mussayev had a Facebook account.

Krasnov had an older brother, the Steele dossier. The Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee paid over $1 million for the research and were fined $113,000 for calling it legal services. John Durham found that the FBI opened its case without “any actual evidence of collusion.” A CIA review faulted John Brennan for pushing it into the 2017 intelligence assessment over the objections of his own Russia experts. In 2020, 51 former intelligence officials saw “all the classic earmarks of a Russian information operation” in the Hunter Biden laptop story. The laptop was real.
Now the deliveries.

Krasnov closed Russia’s consulate in San Francisco, my city. On Sept. 1, 2017, a 95-degree day, black smoke poured from its chimney for hours. Staff told firefighters there was no problem. Whatever was burning, it was not love letters.
Krasnov expelled 60 Russian intelligence officers and closed the Seattle consulate, the largest such expulsion in American history.
Krasnov sanctioned Oleg Deripaska and Viktor Vekselberg. Rusal lost half its market value in a day.
Krasnov sent Ukraine the Javelins former President Barack Obama would not, and approved Georgia’s in November 2017, after years of refusals meant in part to avoid irritating Moscow.

In February 2018, Russian mercenaries joined an assault on American and allied forces near Khasham, Syria. Moscow said no Russians were involved. Then the airstrikes came. Mike Pompeo later said “a couple hundred Russians were killed.”
Krasnov twice bombed Bashar al Assad’s regime, Moscow’s client. The first time, he broke the news to Xi at Mar-a-Lago over “the most beautiful piece of chocolate cake that you’ve ever seen.”

In December 2019, Krasnov signed the sanctions that halted Nord Stream 2; the pipe-layer Allseas walked off the job the next day. In May 2021, the Biden administration waived sanctions on the pipeline’s operator. The pipe never entered service.

The second term was harsher. In October 2025, the Trump Treasury Department sanctioned Rosneft and Lukoil, Russia’s two largest oil companies. When Dmitry Medvedev waved the nuclear card, Trump repositioned two nuclear submarines.

On Jan. 3, Nicolas Maduro began the day in Caracas and ended it in a Brooklyn jail. Russia and Rosneft had lent Caracas at least $17 billion. Four days later, the United States seized a Russian-flagged tanker in the North Atlantic. On Feb. 28, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed on the first day of the American-Israeli war on Iran — Russia’s strategic partner, struck by American bombs.

Then Ukraine. Under NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, allies put up $6.7 billion for American weapons for Kyiv in its first year, and about 95% of the Patriot missiles Ukraine receives come this way. Allies paid. American factories got the orders. Kyiv got missiles, not cash, a wise choice after the $100 million Energoatom kickback scandal.
Now the other column, because a file with one column is not a file. It is a brief.

Helsinki, where Trump took Putin’s word over his own intelligence agencies, three days after Mueller charged 12 Russian military intelligence officers. The call to bring Russia back into the Group of Seven. The 2019 hold on aid to Ukraine that ended in impeachment. The March 2025 pause in weapons and intelligence. The red carpet in Anchorage. A 28-point plan that read, to many, like Moscow’s wish list. And this autumn: the diesel deal; a waiver of the sanctions law named for the late Lindsey Graham, two days before it took effect; the threat to cut off Kyiv’s intelligence unless it stopped hitting Russian refineries; an envoy who called Putin a “humanitarian”; and Putin’s emissary Kirill Dmitriev in the White House.

I read that column twice. I did not find service. I found bargaining. When Trump wants something from Moscow — talks, a prisoner — Moscow gets a carrot. Take the diesel deal. Not a gallon reached an American port by Election Day, and at least three tankers turned away. Putin got a license and no American buyers. Washington got the Russians back at the table in Abu Dhabi. The Graham law’s sponsors said it would give Trump the tools to push Russia to the table. A waiver is a tool, too. When Putin stalls or crosses a line, Moscow gets the stick. Kyiv paused its refinery strikes in October at Trump’s urging, then resumed. By Nov. 10, they had cut Russia’s refining capacity by about 30%, industry sources told Reuters . Some favor to Putin.

Then the love of dictators. The evidence is real. Trump said he and Kim Jong Un “fell in love” over “beautiful letters.” Waiting for Egypt’s Abdel Fattah al Sisi, he reportedly called out, “Where’s my favorite dictator?” Recep Tayyip Erdogan is a friend. Xi is a great leader. Putin is a strong one.

Look closer. In 2017, Kim was “Rocket Man,” promised “fire and fury.” A year later, love. Kim had not changed. Trump’s task had: Pressure had given way to negotiation. His friend Erdogan held an American pastor, so in 2018 Trump sanctioned two Turkish ministers, doubled tariffs on Turkish steel, and got the pastor back. A year later, he reminded his friend in writing of that “little sample” and added: “Don’t be a tough guy. Don’t be a fool!”
For Trump, a compliment is a handshake before the haggling. It costs nothing and opens doors.

Now look at whom he insults. Volodymyr Zelensky, “a dictator without elections.” Germany’s Friedrich Merz, told to stop “interfering” in Iran; the next day, the Pentagon announced it would pull 5,000 troops from Germany. What do they have in common? They depend on America. Dependence invites pressure, and he applies it.

Which brings us back to Shenzhen, and to the choreography I described in these pages on Friday. Protocol in China is a ranking, not a courtesy. Xi went out to the plane for Trump; a Politburo member collected Putin at the airport. When Trump entered the hall, the orchestra played the American anthem. For Putin, it played an excerpt from The Nutcracker. At the welcome banquet, Trump sat beside Xi; Putin, NPR reported, was seated at a separate table. His own aide explained why the two presidents never spoke over the meal: “They did not sit next to each other at the table.” In the group photograph, Xi and Trump stood side by side, and Putin was waved to the far side of Peng Liyuan. The Chinese read power for a living, and they had every reason to flatter Moscow’s man if Moscow had one. They ranked the alleged asset above his alleged handler.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin holds a trilateral meeting with China’s President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump during a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation China Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Andres Martinez Casares/Pool Photo via AP)

The “strong leader” in Moscow watched his pipeline frozen, his oil giants sanctioned, his man in Caracas jailed, and his partner in Tehran killed. Hence the rule: Don’t listen to what Trump says about a man. Watch what he does to the man’s country.

Those of us who grew up in the Soviet Union learned that rule early. “There is no news in Pravda and no truth in Izvestia,” we joked; pravda means truth, and izvestia means news. We read the decrees, not the front page. Americans, raised to take politicians at their word, watch Trump and conclude he has lost his mind. We see a method.
BEIJING RANKED ITS GUESTS IN SHENZHEN. PUTIN CAME SECOND, AND SO DOES HIS BLUFF
The cameras will catch the next handshake too, and Krasnov will trend again. I will be reading the decrees. Nord Stream. Rosneft. Caracas. Tehran .
The file is open. Read it yourself.

Emzari Gelashvili is a San Francisco–based geopolitical analyst and columnist who monitors Russian-language media. From 1996 to 2008, he held senior positions in Georgia’s Ministry of State Security, Ministry of Defense, and Ministry of Internal Affairs, with a counterintelligence career focused on Russian and Iranian intelligence operations, and he was a member of the Georgian Parliament from 2008 to 2012. His work appears in Newsweek, the Hill, the Washington Examiner, RealClearDefense, RealClearWorld, RealClearEducation, and RealClearPolicy, and at emzargelashvili.substack.com.

articles.headline: New Hyundai Elantra Hybrid Debuts With 53 Mpg, AI in the Dash
keyFacts: Hyundai revealed the 2027 Elantra sedan and 2028 Elantra Hybrid at the LA Auto Show with a targeted 53 mpg for the hybrid.
The new models feature the Gleo AI voice assistant, an Android Automotive OS-based dashboard, and a larger exterior design.
Hyundai announced that the 2027 Elantra sedan is expected to arrive in early 2027, followed by the hybrid in late 2027.
body: Hyundai pulled back the cover on the new 2027 Elantra sedan and 2028 Elantra Hybrid this week at the LA Auto Show, and, wow, it looks like nothing else in its class. The bold styling may not be for everyone — though, personally, I dig it — but economy car shoppers will certainly be interested in the compact hybrid sedan’s targeted 53 mpg and Gleo, Hyundai’s new AI voice assistant that controls the automaker’s new Android Automotive OS-based dashboard tech.

The humble Hyundai Elantra hasn’t historically been a sexy car, but it remains an important one for the brand. It’s the automaker’s second-bestselling vehicle, behind only the Tucson. More importantly, the Elantra is one of the stalwarts of the affordable compact sedan class, a segment that many US automakers have abandoned in favor of more profitable SUVs. At a time when buyers are more sensitive than ever to inflated fuel costs and sticker prices, economy car options like the Elantra and its second-generation hybrid powertrain are worth our attention.
More powerful and efficient hybrid

The updated hybrid powertrain pairs a 1.6-liter four-cylinder gasoline engine with a 6-speed dual-clutch automatic gearbox. Combined output at the front wheels rises to 155 horsepower (up from 139 hp in the current car), thanks to a more powerful 45-kilowatt electric-assist motor (up from 32kW).
More from CNET

An updated regenerative braking system recaptures energy when slowing and now offers an “EV-like one-pedal driving experience” that can bring the car to a complete stop at its maximum setting. Additionally, the hybrid now features a new Stay mode that lets the climate control and infotainment systems run while parked for up to 30 minutes without firing up the gas engine.

Sharing the stage in LA, the new nonhybrid Elantra arrives with the same 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine and continuously variable transmission as the current generation. At 147 hp with a target of 35 mpg combined, it’s no more powerful than before, but it should also be no less efficient, despite the sedan’s increased size. I’d say the hybrid is the better choice, though it will likely also be the more expensive powertrain option.
Pleos Connect, Gleo AI

Inside, a new cockpit design moves the now-hoodless digital instrument cluster, a 9.9-inch “Slim Information Display,” away from the driver and toward the windshield on the dashboard. The new placement, similar to what I’ve seen on recent Toyota models, puts vehicle information closer to the driver’s line of sight.

Pleos Connect, Hyundai’s new Android Automotive OS-based infotainment suite, lives on a 12.9-inch center display. Despite being based on Android, it still features the automaker’s bespoke navigation and media software, rather than Google Maps. The system is said to be over-the-air updatable and features standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto for drivers who’d rather bring their own apps on the road.

The Pleos dashboard OS is matched with Gleo AI (who names these things?!), which is Hyundai’s new AI voice assistant that lets drivers and passengers talk to the car rather than occupy a hand on the touchscreen. Hyundai says the system features “contextual language support, multi-command capability and zone-specific recognition,” which basically means the car knows who’s talking to it and which seat they’re in and can assign context to voice prompts based on the situation.
Anything but anonymous

“Affordable doesn’t have to be anonymous,” said Olabisi Boyle, Hyundai’s senior vice president of product, at the unveiling. I agree: Hyundai’s designers clearly aren’t afraid to push the design envelope, and the new Elantra is anything but bland.

The sedan introduces the automaker’s Art of Steel design language, with chunky flared fenders that feel inspired by the brand’s recent new SUVs. The tall greenhouse looks a bit cartoonish if you catch it at the wrong angle, but it provides increased headroom inside. From certain angles, the sedan’s beefy fenders remind me of an angular Korean take on the Subaru WRX. From other viewpoints, I can see inspiration from Hyundai’s N Vision 74 concept and the hydrogen-fueled Nexo, particularly in the triangular rear windows.

The sedan measures 188.8 inches bumper-to-bumper on a 108.3-inch wheelbase that is 1.2 inches longer than the current model’s. Hyundai says the stretch for this generation improves rear-passenger space, now rated at 39.1 inches of legroom on the second row. The Elantra, according to its designers, now approaches the interior volume of a midsize car, a claim I’d take with a grain of salt had I not watched multiple six-foot-plus attendees slip into the back seat with relative ease.
Arriving next year

Hyundai did not announce pricing or detailed specs at the auto show debut, and availability is still vague. However, based on the stated model years, which are usually slightly offset from calendar years, I expect the 2027 Elantra sedan to arrive in early 2027, with the 2028 Elantra Hybrid following in late 2027.
Editors’ note: Antuan Goodwin’s travel costs were covered by Genesis. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

articles.headline: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to kill Ukrainian American rapper on its soil
keyFacts: Danish authorities thwarted an alleged Russian intelligence plot to assassinate Ukrainian American rapper Kyivstoner, the Danish prime minister's office said.
Police arrested two Danish gang members carrying weapons before the concert, and Denmark expelled a Russian defense attaché, officials stated.
The Russian embassy said the accusations lacked proof, while European Union leaders expressed solidarity with Denmark.
body: COPENHAGEN, Denmark — Authorities thwarted the attempted killing of a Ukrainian American citizen on Danish soil in a plot allegedly orchestrated by Russian intelligence services, the Danish prime minister’s office said Friday.

The Russian defense attaché has been expelled from Denmark in response, Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. Two alleged members of the outlawed Danish gang “Loyal to Familia” have been arrested in connection with the attempted killing, police said.
Danish broadcaster DR, citing a court hearing, reported the men are suspected of having been recruited to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper ahead of a planned performance.
Police thwarted the alleged plot when they arrested the two men shortly before the rapper Kyivstoner’s September 25 concert, which was later cancelled.

It was unclear how police identified the two men, who were stopped in a vehicle carrying several weapons, or how the investigation expanded to include two other men who are not accused of participating in the alleged assassination plot targeting Kyivstoner.
However, all four men have been held in custody since September, according to the broadcaster.
It was also unclear how the Russian intelligence services allegedly recruited the two Danish suspects.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said: “It is a clear illustration of the grave security situation Denmark and Europe find ourselves in. We are facing a Russia under pressure which is acting more aggressively and is more willing to take risks.”

The Danes’ announcement came as tensions between Europe and Russia heightened again Friday. Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Saturday the E.U. stands in full solidarity with Denmark.
“This was an attack on E.U. soil. And it is unacceptable. We stand in full solidarity with Denmark. And with all Member States targeted by Russian hybrid attacks,” she said in an X post.
European Council President António Costa said: “We will not be intimidated. Russia’s tactics and threats will not weaken the European Union’s resolve to continue supporting Ukraine.”
The Russian embassy in Copenhagen said on Friday the accusations were not backed with proof.

articles.headline: Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature
keyFacts: Startup GG Technologies sued Apple in an Indian court, alleging that the NameDrop feature infringes its contact-sharing patent.
The startup is seeking ₹15 billion in damages and an injunction to restrict Apple from selling or importing affected devices in India.
The case has not yet been listed for a hearing, and Apple did not respond to a request for comment.
body: Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets users share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.

GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.

Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The company also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims.

In its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The company launched StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024.
Apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1.

“We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing.

In the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale.

Founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android.
Apple did not respond to a request for comment.

India has become increasingly important to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China. The Cupertino company has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth.

articles.headline: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
keyFacts: BBC tests of four major AI chatbots for Black Friday deals found mixed results, including broken retailer links and inaccurate prices.
Consumer group Which? warned that inaccurate chatbot pricing wastes time for Black Friday shoppers trying to find budget deals.
Business advisor Naureen Mohammed said she suspects advertising models will start influencing future chatbot shopping recommendations.
body: - Published
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.
Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.
It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.
Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.
A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.
Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.
But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.
Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.
In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.
But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.
We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.
While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.
ChatGPT - full price and not available to buy
OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.
Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for Â£499 down from Â£649.
The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from Â£379 to Â£814.
Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at Â£649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.
This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.
But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.
The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, Â£150 over our budget and not available online.
At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a Â£1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".
Claude - honest, but not too helpful
Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.
Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.
It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.
But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.
Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.
Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.
It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".
We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.
Gemini - a familiar pattern
Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.
Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.
The prices for one TCL TV were correct at Â£649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.
It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for Â£539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was Â£60 more expensive.
Again, it included two Samsung models to avoid due to lower screen specs.
Alexa - accurate but limited
Alexa came back with four TVs, from its own Amazon Ember at Â£532 to a Â£699 Samsung.
But its top recommendation was to go for another Samsung model at Â£616 (down from Â£749), based on its picture quality and Amazon customer rating.
Its fourth option was for a Sony TV, but it was only 50 inches, leaving us unsure why it had included it.

All the prices stated were correct, but Amazon only searches its own store. Alexa did acknowledge this, encouraging us to check its rivals for better deals, "as prices can vary" and we could get longer guarantees elsewhere.
Inconsistent pricing
There are methods that can boost the likelihood of getting a better response, from crafting more informative prompts to upping a chatbot's "thinking" level.
Tech journalist Alex Hughes had better luck than we did when he used ChatGPT's agentic AI mode to find a TV in last year's Black Friday sales.
Agentic AI is still in its early days, but it allows AI to act with more autonomy and carry out multi-step tasks.
The search took about 20 minutes "with very little work on my end needed," Hughes wrote for Tom's Guide, external in November 2025.
A year on, he told the BBC he didn't go through with buying a TV at that time.
He did later purchase one of the seven models ChatGPT had surfaced - but he had found it for a lower price in a bricks-and-mortar shop.
Will he be using AI to find Black Friday deals again this year? "Probably not," he said.
He reckoned it saved him time, but "when you're trying to deal with something like live price data... it will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect".
Slim pickings
While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.
Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.
If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".
"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.
Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.
Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".
But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under Â£400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.
"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."
